title: AgentOps

techniques.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
techniques.q: Where did this run go wrong?
techniques.what: A trace records one request as a tree of spans: the agent invocation, every model call and every tool call, with timings, token counts, model versions and errors. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, still in Development status, standardise the span and attribute names, so any compatible backend can read them. When quality drops, traces let you group failures by any attribute and find what they share.
use: Any agent in production: you cannot fix what you cannot see
Incidents where the cause could be the model, a tool, a prompt or the data
Cost and latency questions: tokens and time per step, per user, per release
metrics: prompts and outputs are not captured by default; opt in and redact personal data
steps: Set up an OpenTelemetry tracer provider and an OTLP exporter to your backend
Open one root span per request, with child spans for each model and tool call
Record the response model, token usage, finish reason and errors on each span
Query traces grouped by attribute when a metric moves
pitfalls: Logging only the requested model hides a silent provider-side change
Capturing full prompts can store customer personal data in your tracing backend
Sampling away errors: keep every failed trace, sample the successful ones
techniques.remember: One span per step. Record what was served, not just what was asked.
techniques.cap: Illustrative incident: the provider moved an alias to a new snapshot overnight. Only gen_ai.response.model separates the failures.

cmp.scope: Why a run failed, which step, which version

techniques.name: Prompt and Model Versioning
techniques.q: What exactly was running when it broke?
techniques.what: Treat the prompt, the model snapshot, the tool set and the parameters as one versioned release. Pin dated model snapshots instead of aliases the provider can move, keep prompts in a registry with labels such as production and staging, and stamp every trace with the release. Then rollback is a label move, and every trace says exactly what ran.
use: More than one person changes prompts, or prompts change weekly
You depend on a hosted model that is updated or retired on the provider’s schedule
Audits or incidents need to know which prompt produced an answer
metrics: an alias such as claude-sonnet-4-5 can move; a dated snapshot such as claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 does not
numbered versions with labels; code loads by label, not by pasted text
prompt + model + tools + parameters, hashed into one id
the release id on every root span
move the production label back one version; no redeploy
providers deprecate snapshots on a published schedule, so plan migrations
steps: Move prompts out of code into a registry and load them by label
Pin a dated model snapshot in the release configuration
Stamp every trace with the release id
Roll back by moving the label; upgrade snapshots through a canary
pitfalls: An alias in the config lets the provider change your model without a deploy
Prompts edited in a dashboard with no review or eval gate
Pinning forever and missing the retirement date of the snapshot
techniques.remember: Pin the snapshot, label the prompt, stamp the trace.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a release bundles prompt, snapshot, tools and parameters; the provider’s alias moves, the pinned release does not.

cmp.scope: What changed, and how to undo it

techniques.name: Canary Releases and Prompt Flags
techniques.q: How do I ship a change without betting all traffic on it?
techniques.what: Release a new prompt, model or tool version to a small slice of live traffic behind a feature flag, compare it with the control group on the same metrics, and widen in steps, such as 1%, 5%, 25% and 100%, only while guardrail metrics hold. A canary needs enough requests to tell a real drop from noise, so its size and duration come from statistics, not habit.
use: A prompt or model change that passed offline evals but still carries risk
Upgrading to a new model snapshot
High-volume traffic where a bad change would hurt many users quickly
metrics: decides per request which variant runs, sticky per user
hash of a stable id, so a user stays in one group
1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with a bake time at each step
success rate, judge score, latency, cost, escalations
is the canary’s success rate really lower than control’s?
flip the flag off when a guardrail is breached
steps: Pass offline evals first; a canary is the last gate, not the only one
Bucket users by a hash of a stable id and log the variant on every trace
Size the stage so a meaningful drop is detectable, then bake
Widen only while guardrails hold; roll back automatically when one breaks
pitfalls: A canary too small to detect a 4-point drop gives false comfort
Comparing canary and control from different hours or user groups
Per-request randomisation that flips a user between variants mid-conversation
techniques.remember: Small slice, enough samples, widen only while guardrails hold.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: at the 5% stage the canary succeeds on 90.2% of requests against 94.1% for control, so it rolls back.

cmp.best: Canaries too small to see a drop

techniques.name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
techniques.q: Is quality slipping on live traffic right now?
techniques.what: Score live traffic continuously: cheap deterministic checks on every trace, and an LLM judge on a small random sample. Track the scores and the input distribution over time windows, and alert when a score falls below a threshold or the inputs drift. Online evals catch what offline suites cannot: new user behaviour, provider changes and data drift.
use: Any production agent whose inputs or dependencies change over time
Quality that users notice before dashboards do
Offline eval sets that were written months ago
metrics: schema valid, citation present, no PII leaked: run on every trace
an LLM judge on 1–5% of traces, calibrated as in Evaluation
thumbs down, escalations to a human, repeat questions
metric, window, threshold and a minimum sample size
population stability index: under 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, over 0.25 significant
failed live traces become new offline test cases
steps: Run cheap checks on every trace and a judge on a random sample
Aggregate scores in windows with a minimum sample size
Alert on a threshold below the baseline, tuned for few false alarms
Turn every confirmed failure into an offline test case
pitfalls: A window too small to be stable: alerts fire on noise and get ignored
A judge nobody calibrated against human labels
Alerting on averages only, so a failing segment is hidden by the rest
techniques.remember: Check everything cheaply, judge a sample, alert on windows.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a daily judge pass rate on a 2% sample falls from about 92% to 86% after day 7.

techniques.name: Durable Execution and Checkpointing
techniques.q: What happens when the process dies mid-task?
techniques.what: A durable execution engine records the result of every step in an event history, so a workflow that crashes, is redeployed or waits days for a human resumes where it stopped, instead of starting over and repeating side effects. In Temporal, workflow code must be deterministic and all I/O, including model and tool calls, runs in activities with timeouts and retry policies. LangGraph offers a lighter form with checkpointers keyed by a thread id.
use: Long-running agents: minutes to days, with human approvals in between
Steps with side effects: payments, refunds, emails, tickets
Expensive model steps you cannot afford to repeat after a crash
metrics: deterministic orchestration code; replayed from history after a crash
a model call, tool call or API call, with a timeout and retry policy
the recorded result of every completed step
wait for a human approval or a deadline for days, durably
LangGraph saves state after each step; resume with the same thread id
activities run at least once, so side effects still need keys (Tools & MCP)
steps: Put every model and tool call in an activity with a timeout and retry policy
Keep the workflow deterministic: no clocks, random numbers or I/O in it
Wait for approvals with signals or timers, not a sleeping process
Give every side-effecting activity an idempotency key
pitfalls: Non-deterministic workflow code breaks replay
Assuming exactly-once: an activity can run again after a crash
Checkpointing only at the end, so a crash loses all progress
techniques.remember: Record every step. Resume, don’t restart. Keys on side effects.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a ten-step claims job crashes at step 7; the durable version re-runs one step, a plain script all seven.

cmp.scope: Lost progress and repeated side effects

techniques.name: Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Fallbacks
techniques.q: What does the agent do when a provider slows down or fails?
techniques.what: Give every model and tool call a timeout shorter than the user’s patience, stop calling a dependency that keeps failing with a circuit breaker (closed, open, half-open), and route to a fallback: a second provider, a smaller model, a cached answer or a clear message. Tools & MCP makes one call safe to retry; this protects the whole system when a dependency degrades.
use: Any dependency on a hosted model or external API
User-facing latency targets
Traffic high enough that hung calls can exhaust workers
metrics: per call, well below the end-to-end target; the Anthropic and OpenAI Python SDKs default to 10 minutes
the same SDKs retry 2 times by default; add jitter and a retry budget
closed → open after N failures → half-open probe → closed
secondary provider, smaller model, cached answer, graceful message
a separate concurrency limit per dependency
busy workers = request rate × average time per request
steps: Set explicit timeouts and retry counts on every client
Wrap each dependency in a circuit breaker
Define and test a fallback for each critical call
Run outage drills: inject latency and errors, and watch the whole system
pitfalls: Default 10-minute timeouts let hung calls exhaust every worker
Retries without a budget multiply load on a provider that is already failing
Fallback paths that were never tested fail on the day they are needed
techniques.remember: Short timeouts, fail fast, always have a plan B.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a breaker opens after 5 failures, probes after 30 s and sends traffic to a fallback while open.

techniques.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
techniques.q: The agent is misbehaving in production. What now?
techniques.what: When a live agent starts doing harm, you run a practised sequence: detect it from alerts rather than complaints, declare a severity and an owner, contain it with a kill switch or a rollback to the last good release, replay the exact failing trace offline to find the root cause, then turn the failure into an eval case and write a blameless post-mortem. Tracing, versioning, canaries and online evals supply the signals and the levers; this is the playbook that uses them under pressure.
use: An agent that moves money, changes records or messages customers
Any prompt or model change that reaches production, even after a canary
Regulated businesses that must explain, and sometimes report, what went wrong
metrics: alerts on eval scores, tool error spikes and business metrics such as refund rate; user reports are the backstop
SEV1: money or data at risk now; SEV2: degraded; SEV3: minor. Severity sets who is paged and how fast
a kill switch on one tool or the whole agent, then a rollback of prompt and model together to the last good release
the same input, prompt version, model snapshot, parameters and recorded tool responses, run offline with no live calls
the failing trace becomes an eval case that gates every future release; a blameless post-mortem assigns actions, not blame
updates on a fixed rhythm; in India, check early whether a regulator must be told, such as CERT-In’s 6-hour rule for specified cyber incidents
steps: Alert on business and quality signals, with a severity scale and an on-call owner
Contain before you diagnose: flag off the tool, roll back to the last good release
Replay the failing trace with its recorded tool responses to find the root cause
Add the case to the eval set, fix through the normal gate, and write a blameless post-mortem
pitfalls: Hot-fixing the prompt live, without evals, while money is still leaving
Traces without tool responses: a live re-run sees different data and the bug will not reproduce
A post-mortem that blames a person and adds no test, so the same failure ships again
techniques.remember: Alert on money, contain before you debug, replay the exact trace, keep the failure as a test.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Chukta Pay, a fictional Indian payments company, loses about ₹1,000 a minute to duplicate refunds after prompt v8 ships.

cmp.scope: Harm that continues while you work out why
cmp.needs: Alerts, flags, full traces and a runbook
cmp.best: Live hotfixes, and blame instead of tests

techniques.name: User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel
techniques.q: Are users telling us what is broken, and do we act on it?
techniques.what: Users show whether an answer helped far more often through behaviour than through ratings. A feedback loop captures explicit signals (thumbs, ratings, comments) and implicit ones (retries, rephrasing, copying the answer, abandoning, asking for a human, editing a draft), attaches them to the trace of the conversation, and turns them into work: a weekly triage clusters failures into patterns, each pattern becomes eval cases and a fix, and suitable examples become fine-tuning or preference data. That cycle of product use producing better data producing a better product is the data flywheel. Automated scoring of sampled traffic is covered by Online Evals; this technique is about the signals users give and the process that acts on them. Using conversations for training needs a lawful basis, such as notice and consent under India’s DPDP Act, and redaction.
use: Support and sales assistants with high conversation volume
Copilots where users edit drafts before sending
Any product whose eval set has stopped reflecting real use
metrics: thumbs, ratings and comments; rare (1–3% of sessions) and skewed to strong feelings
retry, rephrase, copy, abandon, human handoff, edit distance on drafts
every signal joined to the conversation, prompt version and retrieved context
weekly review that clusters failures into named patterns with counts
days from a pattern appearing to a fix in production
patterns → eval cases, fixes and training data → measured release
steps: Log explicit and implicit signals with the trace id and prompt version
Review a weekly sample of negative signals and cluster them into failure patterns
Turn each pattern into eval cases, then a prompt, retrieval or tool fix
Add consented, redacted examples to training or preference data; measure the next release
pitfalls: Counting thumbs-down alone, which misses most failures
Collecting feedback with no owner or weekly review, so nothing changes
Training on conversations without notice, consent or redaction
techniques.remember: Capture what users do, not only what they rate; triage weekly; turn patterns into evals and fixes.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Dak Mitra, a fictional logistics company, handles 2 lakh support chats a week in English and Hinglish.

cmp.scope: Failures users notice that evals miss
cmp.needs: Signal logging, trace links, a weekly owner
cmp.best: Signals collected but never acted on

from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()                                            #@1
provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter()))   #@1
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)                                    #@1
tracer = trace.get_tracer("claims-copilot")                            #@1

def run_agent(claim_id: str, text: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("invoke_agent claims") as root:  #@2
        root.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "invoke_agent")    #@2
        root.set_attribute("gen_ai.conversation.id", claim_id)         #@2
        policy = call_tool("get_policy", claim_id)
        return call_model(text, policy)

def call_tool(name: str, arg: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"execute_tool {name}") as span:  #@5
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "execute_tool")    #@5
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.tool.name", name)                   #@5
        try:
            return TOOLS[name](arg)
        except Exception as e:
            span.record_exception(e)                                   #@5
            span.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR))      #@5
            raise

def call_model(text: str, policy: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat alpha-latest") as span:    #@3
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")            #@3
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.provider.name", "alpha")            #@3
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", "alpha-latest")     #@3
        r = client.messages.create(model="alpha-latest", max_tokens=800,
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text + policy}])
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.model", r.model)           #@4
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", r.usage.input_tokens)    #@4
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", r.usage.output_tokens)  #@4
        return r.content[0].text

# In the backend: failure rate grouped by gen_ai.response.model    #@6
steps: Set up the tracer
A tracer provider batches spans and exports them over OTLP to any compatible backend: Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Langfuse, Phoenix or a vendor. Your code only talks to the OpenTelemetry API.
Open a root span per request
Each claim gets one invoke_agent span. Every later span nests under it, so the whole run reads as one tree, and the conversation id ties it to the claim.
Wrap each model call
A chat span carries the two required attributes, gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.provider.name, plus the model you asked for. The span name follows the convention: operation, then model.
Record what was served
After the call, record the model that actually answered and the token counts. Here the request said alpha-latest, but the response says alpha-0918: the provider moved the alias.
Wrap each tool call
An execute_tool span names the tool. If it throws, the exception and an ERROR status go on the span, so failures are searchable rather than buried in logs.
Group failures by attribute
When success drops, group failed traces by each attribute in turn. Prompt, tool and region split evenly; gen_ai.response.model does not: 94% on the old snapshot, 84% on the new one.

import mlflow
from opentelemetry import trace

v13 = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(                                     #@1
    name="claims-review",                                               #@1
    template="Summarise the claim. Cite the clause.\n\n{{claim}}",     #@1
    commit_message="Ask for clause citations",                          #@1
    model_config={"model_name": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",  # dated snapshot  #@1,5
                  "temperature": 0.2})                                  #@1

if run_offline_evals("claims-review", v13.version) >= 0.92:             #@2
    mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name="claims-review",                 #@2
                                  alias="production", version=v13.version)  #@2

def summarise(claim: str) -> str:
    p = mlflow.genai.load_prompt("prompts:/claims-review@production")    #@3
    span = trace.get_current_span()
    span.set_attribute("app.prompt.version", p.version)                 #@4
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", p.model_config["model_name"])  #@4,5
    return call_model(p.model_config, p.format(claim=claim))             #@3

def rollback(to_version: int):
    mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name="claims-review",                 #@6
                                  alias="production", version=to_version)  #@6
steps: Register a version
Each change becomes a numbered version with a commit message. The model configuration travels with the prompt, so a version means prompt text and model settings together.
Promote only after evals
The production alias moves to the new version only when the offline suite passes. Nobody edits the live text directly.
Load by alias
Application code asks for claims-review@production. It never contains the prompt text, so promotion needs no redeploy.
Stamp the trace
Every span records the prompt version and the model. When an answer is questioned, the trace says exactly which release produced it.
Pin a snapshot, not an alias
claude-sonnet-4-5 is an alias the provider can move; claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 is a fixed snapshot. Pinning means the model only changes when you change it.
Roll back with one call
If v13 misbehaves, point production back at v12. The next request loads v12; nothing is rebuilt or redeployed.

import hashlib
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

STAGES = [0.01, 0.05, 0.25, 1.0]                                       #@1

def variant(user_id: str, share: float) -> str:
    h = int(hashlib.sha256(user_id.encode()).hexdigest()[:8], 16) / 0xFFFFFFFF  #@2
    return "v13" if h < share else "v12"          # sticky per user     #@2

def handle(user_id: str, stage: int, span):
    v = variant(user_id, STAGES[stage])
    span.set_attribute("app.variant", v)                                #@3
    return run_agent(prompt_version=v)

def decide(canary, control, min_n=350):
    if canary.n < min_n:                                                #@4
        return "bake"                         # not enough evidence yet #@4
    z, p = proportions_ztest([canary.ok, control.ok], [canary.n, control.n],  #@5
                             alternative="smaller")                     #@5
    if p < 0.05 and control.rate - canary.rate > 0.02:                  #@5
        return "rollback"                                               #@5
    return "promote"                                                    #@6

def tick(stage, canary, control):
    d = decide(canary, control)
    if d == "rollback":
        set_share(0.0); page("v13 rolled back")                         #@5
    elif d == "promote":
        stage = min(stage + 1, len(STAGES) - 1)                         #@6
    return stage
steps: Define the ladder
The new prompt goes to 1%, then 5%, 25% and finally everyone. Each stage is a checkpoint where it can still be stopped.
Bucket users, not requests
A hash of the user id gives a number between 0 and 1. Below the share, the user gets v13, and keeps getting it on every request.
Tag every trace with the variant
Online evals, dashboards and alerts can then split every metric by canary and control.
Bake until the evidence is enough
With fewer than about 350 canary requests, a 4-point drop is hard to tell from noise, so the stage waits.
Test, and roll back automatically
A one-sided two-proportion test asks whether the canary is worse. At 5%: 600 requests at 90.2% against 94.1% for control, p < 0.001, so the flag goes to 0%.
Promote stage by stage
If the canary holds, the share moves to the next rung. Each rung repeats the bake and the test.

import math, random
from datetime import timedelta

JUDGE_RATE, WINDOW, MIN_N, MAX_DROP = 0.02, timedelta(hours=6), 200, 0.04  #@1

def on_trace(t):
    store(t.id, "schema_ok", is_valid_json(t.output))                   #@2
    store(t.id, "cited", "[source:" in t.output)                        #@2
    if random.random() < JUDGE_RATE:                                    #@3
        store(t.id, "judge_pass", judge(t.input, t.output))  # calibrated  #@3

def check(now):
    s = scores("judge_pass", since=now - WINDOW)                        #@4
    if len(s) < MIN_N:                                                  #@4
        return                                    # too few to trust   #@4
    rate, base = sum(s) / len(s), baseline("judge_pass")                #@4
    if base - rate > MAX_DROP:                                          #@5
        page(f"judge pass {rate:.1%} vs {base:.1%}", examples=failing(s))  #@5
    ref, cur = intent_mix(days=28), intent_mix(since=now - WINDOW)      #@6
    psi = sum((cur.get(k, 1e-6) - p) * math.log(cur.get(k, 1e-6) / p)   #@6
              for k, p in ref.items())                                  #@6
    if psi > 0.25:                                                      #@6
        page(f"input drift: PSI {psi:.2f}")                             #@6
steps: Choose rate, window and threshold
Judge 2% of traffic, aggregate over 6 hours, require at least 200 judged answers, and alert on a drop of more than 4 points. These four numbers decide how noisy and how fast the alert is.
Cheap checks on every trace
Format and citation checks cost nothing, so they run on every answer and catch hard failures at once.
Judge a random sample
A calibrated LLM judge scores about 1 answer in 50. Random sampling keeps the estimate unbiased; judging everything would cost fifty times more.
Aggregate in a window
Over 6 hours, 2% of 12,500 answers gives 250 judgements: enough for a standard error of about 1.7 points.
Alert with examples
If the pass rate is more than 4 points below baseline, page someone, with links to failing traces so triage starts from evidence.
Watch the inputs too
Compare this window’s intent mix with the last 28 days using the population stability index. Above 0.25 the inputs have shifted, even if scores have not moved yet.

import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from temporalio.worker import Worker

@activity.defn
async def summarise(claim_id: str) -> str:                              #@1
    return await call_model(f"Summarise claim {claim_id}")              #@1

@activity.defn
async def release_payment(claim_id: str, key: str) -> str:              #@6
    return await hospital_api.pay(claim_id, idempotency_key=key)        #@6

@workflow.defn
class CashlessClaim:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.approved = False

    @workflow.signal
    def approve(self) -> None:                                          #@4
        self.approved = True                                            #@4

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, claim_id: str) -> str:
        await workflow.execute_activity(summarise, claim_id,            #@2
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=90),               #@2
            retry_policy=RetryPolicy(maximum_attempts=4))               #@2
        await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approved)            #@4
        return await workflow.execute_activity(release_payment,         #@6
            args=[claim_id, f"pay-{claim_id}"],                         #@6
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30))               #@6

async def main():
    client = await Client.connect("localhost:7233")
    async with Worker(client, task_queue="claims", workflows=[CashlessClaim],  #@3,5
                      activities=[summarise, release_payment]):          #@3,5
        await asyncio.Event().wait()
steps: Put every call in an activity
Model calls, APIs and payments are activities. The workflow only orchestrates them, which keeps it deterministic and replayable.
Timeouts and retries per activity
The summary may take 90 seconds and is retried up to 4 times with backoff. A flaky model call no longer fails the whole claim.
Every result goes into the history
When an activity completes, the server appends its result to the workflow’s event history. That history, not the process memory, is the source of truth.
Wait durably for the surveyor
wait_condition blocks until the approve signal arrives, for minutes or days. No process has to stay alive while it waits.
Crash, replay, continue
If the worker dies during step 7, another worker replays the history: steps 1 to 6 return their recorded results instantly, and the workflow continues waiting for approval.
Key the side effect
Activities run at least once: a crash after the hospital was paid but before the result was recorded retries the payment. The key pay-CL-2291 makes the retry return the first result.

import anthropic, openai, pybreaker

primary = anthropic.Anthropic(timeout=8.0, max_retries=1)              #@1,2
secondary = openai.OpenAI(timeout=8.0, max_retries=0)                   #@1
breaker = pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30)       #@3

@breaker                                                               #@3
def ask_primary(q: str) -> str:
    r = primary.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", max_tokens=600,
                                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])
    return r.content[0].text

def ask_secondary(q: str) -> str:                                       #@4
    r = secondary.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",    #@4
                                          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])
    return r.choices[0].message.content

def answer(q: str) -> str:
    try:
        return ask_primary(q)                                           #@3
    except pybreaker.CircuitBreakerError:                               #@5
        pass                          # open: primary skipped, no wait   #@5
    except Exception:
        pass                          # timeout or error: counted       #@3
    try:
        return ask_secondary(q)                                         #@4
    except Exception:
        return cached_or_message(q)   # cached answer or a clear note   #@6
steps: Set a timeout on every client
Both SDKs wait up to 10 minutes by default. At 20 requests a second, hung calls would hold thousands of workers; 8 seconds bounds the damage.
Keep the retry budget small
The SDKs retry twice by default. One retry on the primary and none on the fallback stops a slow provider from receiving three times the load.
Wrap the dependency in a breaker
pybreaker counts failures. After 5 in a row it opens and stops calling the primary for 30 seconds, then lets one probe through.
Fall back to a second provider
When the primary fails or is skipped, the same question goes to a second provider with its own timeout. Test this path before you need it.
Fail fast while open
An open breaker raises immediately, so requests skip the 8-second wait and go straight to the fallback. Latency stays low during the outage.
Have a last resort
If both providers fail, return a cached answer or a clear message instead of an error page or a hung request.

from ops import open_incident, oncall, set_flag     # your paging and flag services (stubs)
from tracing import load_trace, load_release           # your trace store (stubs)
from refund_agent import run_agent, RecordedTools

BASELINE = 0.021        # refunds per order, 28-day median                 #@1

def check_window(orders: int, refunds: int):
    rate = refunds / max(orders, 1)                                         #@1
    if orders >= 500 and rate > 1.5 * BASELINE:                              #@1
        open_incident(sev="SEV1", title=f"refund rate {rate:.1%}",           #@2
                      owner=oncall("payments-agents"))                        #@2

def contain():
    set_flag("refund_agent.issue_refund", False)   # kill switch: refunds queue for people  #@3
    set_flag("refund_agent.release", "rel-v7")     # prompt v7 and the snapshot it shipped with  #@3

def replay(trace_id: str):
    tr = load_trace(trace_id)
    release = load_release(tr.release_id)          # prompt v8, snapshot, temperature 0  #@4
    tools = RecordedTools(tr.tool_calls)           # recorded responses, no live calls   #@4
    out = run_agent(tr.input, release=release, tools=tools)                  #@4
    return [c for c in out.tool_calls if c.name == "issue_refund"]           #@5

refunds = [len(replay("tr-4f91")) for _ in range(10)]
assert refunds == [2] * 10     # reproduced: PENDING read as "not refunded"  #@5

EVAL_SET.append({"trace": "tr-4f91",                                          #@6
                 "expect": {"issue_refund_calls": 1}})    # v8 fails, v7 passes  #@6
gate_release("rel-v9", eval_set=EVAL_SET)                  # the fix ships through the gate  #@6
steps: Alert on a business metric

The refund rate per 10-minute window is watched against its 28-day median of 2.1%. The alert fires above 1.5 × 2.1% = 3.15%, and only when at least 500 orders are in the window. At 10:10 the window holds 40 refunds on 900 orders, 4.4%, so the page goes out at 10:12, 12 minutes after prompt v8 went live. Waiting for complaints would have taken about four hours.
Declare a severity and an owner

Money is leaving at about ₹1,000 a minute, so this is SEV1: page now, one incident commander, one channel, one timeline. The commander decides; others investigate. A severity scale agreed in advance removes the argument about how serious it is.
Contain before you diagnose

At 10:17 a flag turns off the issue_refund tool, so new refunds queue for people instead of being paid. Then the release flag moves back to rel-v7: prompt v7 with the model snapshot it was tested with. Nobody edits the prompt live; a guess made under pressure, without evals, can make things worse.
Replay the exact trace

Trace tr-4f91 holds the customer’s input, the release id and every tool call with its response. The replay loads prompt v8, the same pinned snapshot and parameters, and serves the recorded responses instead of calling live APIs, so no real refund can go out. A live re-run now would see refund_status return SUCCESS and never show the bug.
Find the root cause

The replay calls issue_refund twice in all 10 runs. Prompt v8 added “if the refund is not confirmed, issue it again”; the gateway reports PENDING for up to 90 seconds, which the agent read as not refunded. A contributing cause: issue_refund had no idempotency key per order, so the second call was paid too.
Keep the failure as a test

The trace becomes an eval case that expects exactly one issue_refund call. v8 fails it and v7 passes it, and the fix, rel-v9, ships only through the gate. The blameless post-mortem records the timeline, ₹17,000 lost, the causes and owned actions, such as adding the idempotency key.

from langfuse import get_client
lf = get_client()

def on_thumbs(trace_id, up, comment=None):                                   #@1
    lf.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name="user_thumbs", value=1 if up else 0,
                    comment=comment)

def on_event(trace_id, kind):          # retry, rephrase, handoff, copy     #@2
    lf.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name=f"implicit_{kind}", value=1)

def weekly_triage(week):                                                     #@3
    bad = fetch_traces(week, any_of=["user_thumbs=0", "implicit_retry",
                                     "implicit_handoff"], sample=300)
    patterns = cluster_and_label(bad)   # human reviewer names each cluster  #@3
    for p in patterns[:5]:
        eval_set.add(p.examples[:20], tag=p.name)                            #@4
        open_ticket(p.name, owner="assistant-team")                          #@4
    consented = [t for t in bad if t.consent_training and redact_ok(t)]      #@5
    training_queue.add(consented)
    return patterns

# 8 weeks: first-contact resolution 72% → 79%; fix time 45 → 10 days      #@6
steps: Capture explicit feedback
Dak Mitra, a fictional logistics company, adds thumbs to its support chat. Only about 1.5% of 2 lakh weekly chats get a rating, mostly from very unhappy or very happy users.
Capture what users do
Retries, rephrasing, copying the tracking answer and asking for a human are logged as implicit signals on the same trace. They are noisy, but there are ten times more of them.
Triage every week
A reviewer samples 300 negative traces, clusters them and names the patterns: “COD refund status in Hinglish”, “pincode not serviceable”, “wrong courier partner”.
Turn patterns into evals and fixes
The top five patterns each add 20 eval cases and get an owner. A fix ships only when those cases pass.
Feed the flywheel carefully
Only conversations with training consent and clean redaction go to the training queue, in line with DPDP notice and consent.
Measure the loop
After eight weeks, first-contact resolution rises from 72% to 79%, and the time from a pattern appearing to its fix falls from 45 to 10 days.

lib: Vendor-neutral tracing. The opentelemetry-instrumentation-openai-v2 package emits GenAI spans for OpenAI calls automatically; you add spans for your own agent and tools.
code:
import os
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.openai_v2 import OpenAIInstrumentor
from openai import OpenAI

# Opt in to the latest (still experimental) GenAI conventions; keep content capture off.
os.environ.setdefault("OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN", "gen_ai_latest_experimental")

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter()))  # OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
OpenAIInstrumentor().instrument()              # emits a "chat {model}" span per call

tracer = trace.get_tracer("claims-copilot")
client = OpenAI()

def summarise(claim_id: str, text: str) -> str:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("invoke_agent claims-copilot") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "invoke_agent")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.agent.name", "claims-copilot")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.conversation.id", claim_id)
        span.set_attribute("app.release", "cfg-7f3a")       # your own release id
        r = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
                                           messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content
tracing.note: Auto-instrumentation records gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.response.model for you. Query your backend for failure rate grouped by gen_ai.response.model when quality moves.

import mlflow

# Register a new version (the template uses {{double braces}})
p = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name="claims-review",
    template="Summarise this claim for the desk. Cite the policy clause.\n\n{{claim}}",
    commit_message="Add clause citation",
    model_config={"model_name": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",   # a pinned snapshot
                  "temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 800},
)

# Promote it after offline evals pass
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name="claims-review", alias="production", version=p.version)

# Application code loads by alias, never by pasted text
prompt = mlflow.genai.load_prompt("prompts:/claims-review@production")
text = prompt.format(claim="Hospitalisation, 3 days, cashless request ...")
model = prompt.model_config["model_name"]

# Rollback: point the alias at the previous version; no redeploy
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name="claims-review", alias="production", version=p.version - 1)
versioning.note: Record the prompt name, version and model snapshot on every trace so an incident can be tied to one release.

from openfeature import api
from openfeature.evaluation_context import EvaluationContext
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

flags = api.get_client()          # configure a provider (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, flagd...) at startup

def pick_prompt(user_id: str) -> str:
    ctx = EvaluationContext(targeting_key=user_id)          # sticky per user
    return flags.get_string_value("refund-prompt-version", "v12", ctx)

def canary_is_worse(ok_canary, n_canary, ok_control, n_control, max_drop=0.02):
    """One-sided test: is the canary's success rate lower than control's?"""
    z, p = proportions_ztest([ok_canary, ok_control], [n_canary, n_control],
                             alternative="smaller")
    drop = ok_control / n_control - ok_canary / n_canary
    return p < 0.05 and drop > max_drop

# 1,200 canary conversations at 90.2% vs 22,800 control at 94.1%
print(canary_is_worse(1082, 1200, 21455, 22800))   # True: roll back

code:
import math, random
from langfuse import get_client

langfuse = get_client()
JUDGE_RATE = 0.02

def on_answer(trace_id: str, question: str, answer: str):
    langfuse.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name="has_citation",
                          value=1.0 if "[source:" in answer else 0.0)
    if random.random() < JUDGE_RATE:                       # judge a random sample
        verdict = judge(question, answer)                  # your calibrated LLM judge
        langfuse.create_score(trace_id=trace_id, name="judge_pass",
                              value=1.0 if verdict else 0.0)

def psi(expected: dict, actual: dict, eps=1e-6) -> float:
    """Population stability index between two category distributions."""
    return sum((actual.get(k, eps) - e) * math.log(actual.get(k, eps) / e)
               for k, e in expected.items())

def should_page(pass_rate, baseline, n, min_n=200, max_drop=0.04):
    return n >= min_n and baseline - pass_rate > max_drop

lib: One interface over many providers, with per-call timeouts, retries, fallbacks and cooldowns for failing deployments.
code:
from litellm import Router

router = Router(
    model_list=[
        {"model_name": "primary",
         "litellm_params": {"model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", "timeout": 8}},
        {"model_name": "secondary",
         "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-4o-2024-08-06", "timeout": 8}},
    ],
    fallbacks=[{"primary": ["secondary"]}],   # used after primary fails
    num_retries=1,                            # small retry budget
    allowed_fails=3,                          # failures before cooldown
    cooldown_time=30,                         # seconds out of rotation
)

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    try:
        r = router.completion(model="primary",
                              messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content
    except Exception:
        return "Order status is delayed right now. Please check the order book in the app."

lib: A few lines of pandas turn exported signals into a weekly failure-pattern table; any tracing tool can export them.
code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.read_csv("signals.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])        # trace_id, ts, kind, pattern
week = s[s.ts >= s.ts.max() - pd.Timedelta(days=7)]

negative = week[week.kind.isin(["thumbs_down", "retry", "rephrase", "handoff"])]
print("traces with a negative signal:", negative.trace_id.nunique())

table = (negative.dropna(subset=["pattern"])
         .groupby("pattern").trace_id.nunique()
         .sort_values(ascending=False).head(5))
print(table)                                              # top five failure patterns
table.to_csv("patterns_this_week.csv")

The time within which 95% of requests finish.

incident.scenario: Chukta Pay, a fictional Indian payments company, ships refund-agent prompt v8 at 10:00. From then on the agent pays about 40 duplicate refunds an hour, averaging ₹1,500 each: ₹1,000 a minute. You choose how the problem is detected, how you respond, what your traces captured and whether the failure becomes an eval case. The day is counted as 24 hours from the deploy.
controls: Choose detection: wait for merchant complaints (about 4 hours) or alert on a refund-rate anomaly (12 minutes).
Choose the response: hot-fix the prompt live (40 minutes, stops 75% of duplicates) or flip the kill switch and roll back to v7 (5 minutes).
Choose trace capture, logs only or full traces with tool responses, and tick whether the failing case joins the eval set. Or load a scenario.
outputs: Minutes from the v8 deploy until the on-call engineer knows.
Minutes from detection until duplicate refunds fully stop, or not within the day.
Duplicate refunds paid: ₹1,000 a minute until containment, ₹250 a minute while a partial hotfix is live.
Whether a deterministic replay with recorded tool responses reproduces the double refund.
Illustrative chance the same failure ships again within 6 months: 5% with the cause found and an eval case, 35% with the cause but no case, 50% with a case but no cause, 60% with neither.

tracing.title: Recording the model on a chat span
tracing.code:
with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat alpha-latest") as span:
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", MODEL)
    r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=800, messages=msgs)
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.model", MODEL)
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", r.usage.output_tokens)
tracing.explain: The response model is copied from the request, so every span says alpha-latest even after the provider moves the alias to a new snapshot. Grouping failures by served model then shows nothing, and the overnight change stays invisible.

also.3: Correct: the requested model is what you asked for, and it is worth recording too.
also.6: Correct: token usage comes from the response, as it should.

versioning.title: A release configuration
versioning.explain: claude-sonnet-4-5 is a model alias, which the provider can point at a new snapshot at any time. The release then changes without any deploy on your side, which is exactly how an overnight drop with no deploy happens.

also.2: Correct: loading the prompt by your own registry label is intended; you control when that label moves.
also.4: Correct: generation parameters belong in the release.

canary.title: Assigning users to the canary
canary.code:
import hashlib, random

def variant(user_id: str, share: float) -> str:
    h = random.random()
    return "v13" if h < share else "v12"
canary.explain: A fresh random number on every request means a user can get v13 on one message and v12 on the next. Conversations mix variants, users see inconsistent behaviour, and metrics cannot be attributed to either version.

also.5: Correct: users below the share get the canary; the logic is fine once h is stable per user.

onlineeval.title: The quality alert rule
onlineeval.explain: The subtraction is the wrong way round: it pages when the pass rate rises more than 4 points above baseline and stays silent when it falls. A real drop never triggers the alert.

also.2: Correct: a minimum sample size stops alerts firing on a handful of judgements.
also.4: Correct: the pass rate is the mean of the 0/1 judge scores.

durable.title: A Temporal workflow that waits overnight
durable.explain: Workflow code is replayed after a crash, and datetime.now() returns a different time on replay, so the workflow can take a different branch than it did originally and no longer match its history. Use the deterministic workflow clock.

also.4: Correct: inside a Temporal workflow, asyncio.sleep becomes a durable timer.
also.5: Correct: the model call runs as an activity with a timeout.

resilience.title: A client with a circuit breaker
resilience.explain: The SDK timeout is in seconds, not milliseconds, so 8000 means more than two hours: even longer than the 10-minute default. Hung calls hold workers until the pool is exhausted, and the breaker only counts failures after they finally time out.

also.3: Correct: open after 5 failures, probe again after 30 seconds.
also.5: Correct: the decorator routes each call through the breaker.

incident.title: A kill switch for the refund tool
incident.explain: The flag is read once, when the module is imported, and the result is kept in REFUNDS_ON. Flipping the kill switch during an incident changes nothing until every process restarts, so duplicate refunds keep going out while the team believes the tool is off.

also.1: Correct: one flag client for the process is fine; it is the value that must be read per call.
also.7: Correct: an idempotency key per order stops a second refund for the same order from being paid.

feedback.title: Weekly triage query
feedback.explain: Only thumbs-down traces are triaged. With ratings on 1.5% of chats, most failures show up only as retries, rephrasing or handoffs, so the patterns miss them.

also.3: Clustering and naming patterns is right.
also.5: Adding 20 cases per pattern to the eval set is right.

2: A claim arrives. What does the root span represent?
The whole agent run for this claim
Only the first model call
The invoke_agent span covers the whole run, and every model and tool span nests under it.
3: Which attributes are required on the chat span?
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens
gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.provider.name
Those two are required; the model and token attributes are recommended.
4: The request asked for alpha-latest. What does the response say?
alpha-latest, always
The snapshot that actually served it: alpha-0918
The provider resolves the alias; only the response model shows which snapshot answered.
5: The policy tool throws. What should the span show?
Nothing: the exception is enough
The exception and an ERROR status
Recording the exception and status makes the failure searchable in the trace backend.
6: Which grouping will split the failures?
gen_ai.response.model
Region
Prompt, tool and region all sit near 86%; the served model splits 94% from 84%.

2: When does production move to v13?
As soon as it is registered
Only after the offline evals pass
Registration creates a version; promotion is a separate, gated step.
3: How does the app get its prompt text?
By loading the production alias from the registry
From a string in the code
Loading by alias means promotion and rollback need no redeploy.
4: What should each trace record?
The prompt version and the model snapshot
Only the user’s question
Those two identify the release that produced the answer.
5: Which model name protects you from silent changes?
claude-sonnet-4-5
claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929
The dated name is a fixed snapshot; the short one is an alias the provider can move.
6: v13 misbehaves. What is the fastest rollback?
Revert the commit and redeploy
Point the production alias at v12
Moving the alias takes effect on the next request, with no build or deploy.

2: User 42 lands in v13. What do they get on their next message?
v13 again
A new random draw
Hashing a stable id makes assignment sticky, so each user sees one version.
3: Why tag each trace with the variant?
So every metric can be split by canary and control
To make traces smaller
Without the tag, online evals and dashboards cannot compare the two groups.
4: The canary has 310 conversations. What happens?
Promote: nothing bad seen so far
Keep baking: too little evidence
Below about 350, a 4-point drop is hard to tell from noise.
5: 600 conversations at 90.2% against 94.1% for control. What does the test say?
Not significant, keep going
Significantly worse: roll back
The drop is about 3 standard errors, p < 0.001, and bigger than the 2-point tolerance.
6: The canary holds at 5%. What comes next?
Straight to 100%
25%, with another bake
Each rung repeats the bake and the test; widening in steps limits exposure.

2: Which checks run on every answer?
The LLM judge
Cheap deterministic checks such as format and citations
Deterministic checks cost almost nothing, so they run on everything; the judge is sampled.
3: How are answers chosen for the judge?
At random, about 1 in 50
The longest answers first
Random sampling keeps the estimate unbiased.
4: The window has 120 judged answers. Does the rule compute a rate and compare?
Yes, any sample will do
No: below 200 it returns without alerting
A minimum sample size keeps noise from paging people.
5: The pass rate is 86% against a 92% baseline. What happens?
A page, with links to failing traces
Nothing until the daily report
A 6-point drop exceeds the 4-point threshold, so the rule pages with examples.
6: Scores are steady, but the intent mix shifted: PSI 0.29. Is that worth an alert?
No, only scores matter
Yes: the inputs changed, and scores may follow
Above 0.25 is a significant shift; it often precedes a quality drop on new kinds of request.

2: The summary call times out once. What happens?
The activity is retried with backoff
The whole claim fails
The retry policy allows up to 4 attempts, so one timeout is absorbed.
3: Where is the summary’s result kept?
Only in the worker’s memory
In the workflow’s event history on the server
The history is the source of truth that survives crashes.
4: The surveyor takes two days. What is running meanwhile?
A process sleeping for two days
Nothing: the workflow waits durably for a signal
wait_condition parks the workflow; no process has to stay alive.
5: The worker dies during step 7. Where does the new worker resume?
At step 7, after replaying steps 1–6 from history
At step 1
Replay returns the recorded results of completed steps and continues from there.
6: The payment succeeded, then the worker crashed before recording it. What prevents a second payment?
Nothing: Temporal guarantees exactly once
The idempotency key the hospital API honours
Activities run at least once, so the key is what makes the retry safe.

2: Why reduce retries on the primary?
Retries add load to a provider that is already failing
Retries are free
Each retry is another request to a struggling dependency; budgets prevent retry storms.
3: The primary fails 5 times in a row. What does the breaker do?
Keeps calling it
Opens and stops calling it for 30 s
An open breaker fails fast, then probes after the reset timeout.
4: The primary call failed. Where does the question go?
Back to the user as an error
To the secondary provider
The fallback gives the user an answer from another provider.
5: The breaker is open. How long does a request wait for the primary?
About 0.01 s: it is skipped
8 s: it waits for the timeout
Failing fast is what keeps latency low during an outage.
6: Both providers fail. What should the user see?
A cached answer or a clear message
A spinner until the request times out
A last resort beats an error page or a hung request.

2: Money is leaving at about ₹1,000 a minute. Which severity fits?
SEV1: page now, one incident commander
SEV3: look at it tomorrow morning
Harm happening now, with money leaving every minute, is the top severity: page immediately and put one person in charge.
3: The cause is not known yet. What comes first?
Edit the prompt live to forbid repeat refunds
Turn off the refund tool, then roll back to rel-v7
Contain before you diagnose. A kill switch and a rollback to a tested release stop the harm without guessing under pressure.
4: Why serve recorded tool responses in the replay?
A live call now returns SUCCESS and could pay a real refund
Recorded responses make the replay faster, nothing more
The recorded PENDING response is what triggered the bug, and replays must never touch live payment systems.
5: The replay calls issue_refund twice in 10 of 10 runs. What does that show?
The failure reproduces, so the cause can be studied and tested
The model is random and the incident cannot be explained
A failure that reproduces on replay is a bug with a cause, here the new prompt instruction plus the missing idempotency key.
6: What stops the same failure shipping again next quarter?
A reminder in the post-mortem to be careful
An eval case that fails any release paying this ticket twice
Post-mortem actions fade; a test in the release gate keeps running on every future prompt and model.

2: Which signal is most common?
Implicit behaviour such as retries
Written comments
About ten times more than ratings.
3: What does a weekly triage produce?
Named failure patterns with counts
A new model
Patterns are the unit of work.
4: When does a fix ship?
When the pattern’s eval cases pass
When the reviewer likes it
Eval cases guard the fix.
5: Which conversations may go to training data?
Consented and redacted ones
All of them
DPDP notice and consent.
6: Resolution after eight weeks?
Up 7 points; fixes in 10 days.

tracing: A claims copilot’s success rate fell 8 points overnight with no deploy. Spans record only the model name sent in the request, the alias alpha-latest. Which attribute would most directly reveal a provider-side model change?
The response model is the snapshot that actually served the call; the request only shows the alias you asked for.
A bank is adopting the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for its loan assistant. Which pair of attributes is required on a chat span?
Operation and provider are required; model and token attributes are recommended, and message content is opt-in.
Following the GenAI span naming convention, what should a chat call to a model named beta-2 be called?
Chat spans are named by operation then model: “chat {model}”. invoke_agent names the agent’s root span.

An order-support agent’s root span lasts 5.0 s. Its children run one after another: a chat span of 1.8 s, a tool span of 0.4 s and a chat span of 2.1 s. How much of the root span is not covered by child spans?
1.8 + 0.4 + 2.1 = 4.3 s, so 5.0 − 4.3 = 0.7 s is spent outside the recorded calls.
A returns agent is being instrumented. Which should be recorded on every model span by default? Select all that apply.
The model that served the call
The full prompt, including the customer’s address
The whole conversation history as one attribute
Tokens and the served model are cheap and essential. Prompt content can hold personal data and stays off unless you opt in with redaction.
A hospital’s discharge-summary agent handles patient notes. The team wants traces for debugging. What is the best default for message content?
Capture all prompts and outputs, since the backend is internal
Put the prompt text into span names for easy search
Keep content capture off, record metadata, and enable redacted content only where needed
Do not trace this agent at all
Metadata such as models, tokens, timings and errors gives most of the debugging value without storing patient data.
A telecom support agent produces 2 million traces a day, and storing them all is too expensive. Which sampling policy keeps the most diagnostic value?
Keep every error trace and a sample of successful ones
Keep 1% of all traces, chosen uniformly
Keep only traces from the first hour of each day
Errors are rare and the most useful for diagnosis, so keep them all and sample the successful majority.
A delivery agent’s failures are grouped by attribute. By served model: every group is near 90%. By tool: get_eta traces succeed 61%, all others 93%. What is the most likely cause?
The get_eta tool or the API behind it
Only the tool dimension splits the failures, which points at get_eta, not at the model.
A rebooking agent’s seat-hold tool throws an exception. What should its execute_tool span record so the failure is searchable?
Nothing; the stack trace in stdout is enough
A new root span for the error
The exception, plus an ERROR status on the span
The exception text in the span name
Recording the exception and setting the status makes failed tool calls filterable in any trace backend.
A span records 3,000 input and 500 output tokens. Input costs $3 and output $15 per million tokens. What does this call cost?
Traces show success grouped by served model: alpha-0712 at 94% on 20% of traffic and alpha-0918 at 84% on 80%. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
Rolling back the prompt is the most likely fix
0.2 × 94 + 0.8 × 84 = 86%. The split is by served model, so pinning the old snapshot fixes it; prompt and region are not implicated.
A KYC agent’s trace shows a root span but no child spans, so nobody can tell which step is slow. What is missing?
Spans around each model call and tool call, nested under the root
Without child spans the trace has no step structure; each model and tool call needs its own span.
Why use the standard gen_ai.* attribute names instead of inventing your own, such as llm_model?
They are required for the model to work
Any compatible backend and tool can read and chart them without custom mapping
Standard names are what make traces portable across backends and dashboards.
A bank wants to see where tokens go in its dispute agent. Which trace-based analyses help? Select all that apply.
Sum input and output tokens per span name
Compare tokens per step across releases
Count spans per trace to find loops
Read only the final answer text
Token attributes per span show which steps cost most, how releases change that, and whether runs loop; the final answer alone shows none of it.
The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions are in which status as of 2026?
Development, so names can still change
Only a draft proposal with no implementations
They are widely implemented but still in Development, which is why instrumentations offer an opt-in for the latest version.
An agent calls a moving alias. The same request model appears on every span for months. What does that tell you about the snapshot that served each call?
Nothing: only the response model shows the served snapshot
That the provider pinned it for you
The request carries the alias name every time, whichever snapshot the provider actually used.
An on-call engineer must find the cause of a quality drop quickly. Which trace attributes are worth grouping by first? Select all that apply.
Model and release are the usual suspects for sudden drops; timestamps and random ids do not form meaningful groups.
A payments agent’s p95 latency doubled. Traces show chat spans unchanged but execute_tool fraud_score spans went from 0.3 s to 2.4 s. Where should the fix start?
The fraud_score tool or its API
The step whose duration changed is the tool call, so that is where the latency comes from.
A team exports spans synchronously after each model call, and request latency rose by 40 ms. What is the usual fix?
Use a batch span processor that exports in the background
Put all attributes in the span name
A batch processor queues spans and exports them off the request path.
A health-tech firm must trace an agent handling patient queries under India’s data protection rules. Which practices fit? Select all that apply.
Redact personal data before any content is stored
Restrict access to traces that contain content
Keep traces with content forever for convenience
Send full prompts to a third-party backend by default
Redaction and access control limit exposure; unlimited retention and default content export increase it.
versioning: A portfolio assistant’s config says model: claude-sonnet-4-5. Why is this risky in production?
It is an alias, which the provider can point at a new snapshot without your deploy
An alias can move; a dated snapshot such as claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 stays fixed until you change it.
A bank’s letter-drafting prompt lives as a string in the code. A bad edit ships. What is the main cost of this setup during rollback?
A code change and redeploy are needed to undo it
With prompts in code, rollback is a deploy; with a registry, it is a label move.
Which set of items should one versioned agent release bundle?
The prompt and the user’s question
Prompt version, model snapshot, tool definitions and generation parameters
The trace backend and the dashboard
Anything that changes behaviour belongs in the release, so an answer can be tied to exactly what produced it.
A provider starts serving a new snapshot behind your alias to 60% of traffic. The old snapshot succeeds 95% of the time and the new one 85%. What is your overall success rate?
A SaaS team moves prompts to a registry. Which practices make that worthwhile? Select all that apply.
Load prompts in code by label, such as production
Promote a new version only after evals pass
Let anyone edit the live production text directly
Copy the prompt text into each service for speed
Loading by label and gated promotion give fast, safe rollout; direct edits and copies bypass the registry.
A team pins a dated snapshot. What ongoing work does that create?
None; pinned snapshots are supported forever
Tracking the snapshot’s retirement date and planning upgrades
Providers retire snapshots on a schedule, so pinned releases need planned migrations.
An auditor asks which prompt produced a customer letter sent three weeks ago. What makes this answerable in seconds?
The release id, including the prompt version, stamped on the trace for that request
Asking the engineer who wrote the prompt
A release stamp on each trace ties every output to the exact prompt and model version.
In MLflow’s prompt registry, how does application code usually load the live prompt?
By the alias URI, such as prompts:/claims-review@production
By pasting the latest text into the code
By version number hard-coded in every service
By downloading it from the trace backend
Loading by alias lets promotion and rollback happen by moving the alias.
A clinical-summary team needs to roll back a bad prompt quickly and prove what ran. Which do they need? Select all that apply.
A registry with numbered versions and a production label
The prompt version recorded on every trace
Versions plus labels give fast rollback; trace stamps give proof. Model size and examples are unrelated.
Prompt v13 is live and misbehaving. Using a registry with aliases, what is the fastest safe rollback?
Point the production alias back at version 12
Moving the alias restores v12 on the next request and keeps v13 for investigation.
Why store the model configuration, such as snapshot and temperature, with the prompt version?
Prompts only work with one temperature
A prompt tuned for one model and setting can behave differently on another, so they change together
Prompt and model settings interact, so versioning them together keeps a release reproducible.
A bank’s agent broke after the provider changed the model behind its alias. Which measures would have prevented or shortened this? Select all that apply.
Recording the served model on traces
Pinning prevents the silent change; recording the served model makes it visible at once.
An EdTech company changes its tutoring prompt weekly. Which statement about using Git alone for prompts is correct?
It gives review and history, but rollback still needs a deploy
It rolls back instantly without a deploy
It records which snapshot served each request
Git gives history and review; runtime label moves need a registry or config service.
A team upgrades to a new model snapshot. What is the right order?
Run offline evals, canary the new snapshot, then promote
Change the alias and wait for complaints
Offline evals catch known problems, the canary catches live ones, and only then does everyone get it.
Which of these change an agent’s behaviour and should therefore be part of its versioned release? Select all that apply.
The tool definitions and their descriptions
The colour of the admin dashboard
Tool descriptions and parameters change what the model does; rotas and dashboards do not.
A release record is hashed into one id, cfg-7f3a. What is the main benefit?
One short id on every trace identifies the whole configuration that ran
A single id makes filtering traces and comparing releases simple.
Three teams edit the same support prompt in a shared dashboard, and a bad edit went live on a Friday. What is the best process fix?
Let only one engineer edit prompts
Any edit creates a version; promotion to production needs review and passing evals
Versioned drafts keep teams fast, while gated promotion keeps production safe.
A fintech wants every answer traceable to what produced it. Which three things together make that true? Select all that apply.
The release stamped on every trace
All three are needed: the prompt version, a fixed model and the stamp that records them.
A pinned snapshot is announced for retirement in 60 days. What should the team do?
Evaluate the replacement offline, canary it, and promote before the date
Remove the model from the release
Retirements are scheduled, so migrate deliberately through evals and a canary.
An incident timeline shows: 90 minutes to find which prompt was live, 45 minutes to redeploy. Which changes cut both? Select all that apply.
Stamping the prompt version on traces
Loading prompts from a registry by label
The stamp removes the search; the registry replaces the redeploy with a label move.
canary: A new refund prompt passed offline evals. How should it reach users?
To everyone at once, since evals passed
To a small share behind a flag, compared with control, then widened in steps
Randomly to half of all requests with no comparison
A canary is the last gate: a small slice, a concurrent control and gradual widening.
A telecom’s plan-recommendation agent gets 2,000 conversations an hour. A canary runs at 5% for 6 hours. How many canary conversations is that?
In that 600-conversation canary, the new prompt is truly 3 points worse. How many extra failed conversations did the canary cause?
600 × 0.03 = 18, against 360 if the whole service had run it for the same 6 hours.
Why should canary assignment hash a stable user id rather than draw a random number per request?
It hides the variant from logs
So each user sees one version consistently and metrics can be attributed
Random numbers are not allowed in Python
Per-request draws mix versions within a conversation and blur the comparison.
A canary’s success rate is compared with the control group. Which practices make the comparison valid? Select all that apply.
Control and canary run over the same period
The variant is recorded on every trace
Compare the canary with last month’s average
Put all premium users in the canary
A concurrent control and variant tags make groups comparable; old baselines and biased assignment do not.
A canary of 40 conversations shows 90% success against 94% for control. What should you conclude?
The new version is worse; roll back
The sample is too small to tell a 4-point difference from noise
With 40 conversations the standard error is about 4.7 points, as large as the difference itself.
Roughly how many canary conversations are needed to detect a drop from 94% to 90% with about 80% power in a one-sided test?
n ≈ ((1.645 + 0.84) × 0.3 / 0.04)² ≈ 350 when the control group is large.
Why does proving a 1-point improvement take far more traffic than catching a 4-point drop?
The required sample grows with the inverse square of the difference, so a quarter of the effect needs about sixteen times the data
It does not; both need the same sample
Halving the effect quadruples the sample; a 1-point gain needs about sixteen times more than a 4-point drop.
Which metrics make sensible guardrails for a rebooking-prompt canary? Select all that apply.
Number of lines in the prompt
Guardrails are live outcome metrics such as success, latency, cost and escalations.
A broker’s canary guardrail is breached at 2 a.m. What should happen?
Widen the canary to get more data
Page someone to edit the prompt live
The flag turns the canary off automatically and alerts the owner
Automatic rollback limits harm; the investigation can happen after.
Which is the typical order of canary stages?
Start small and widen in steps, baking and checking at each one.
A health app has only 300 conversations a day. Which statements about canarying there are correct? Select all that apply.
A canary may never reach a meaningful sample in reasonable time
Stronger offline evals and careful review matter more
A 1% canary for one hour is enough
Canary statistics work the same at any traffic level
Low traffic makes live comparisons slow and noisy, so offline evidence must carry more weight.
Which tool provides a vendor-neutral feature-flag API with pluggable providers?
OpenFeature standardises flag evaluation; LaunchDarkly, Unleash and others plug in as providers.
Argo Rollouts canaries a new agent image by shifting pods. What can it not do on its own that a prompt flag can?
Keep each user on one variant across requests
Pod-level canaries route requests, not users; per-user stickiness needs a flag or routing on a user key.
A KYC-extraction prompt canary shows a higher manual-review rate but the same accuracy. Which actions are sensible? Select all that apply.
Treat manual-review rate as a guardrail and roll back if it breaches
Investigate which documents trigger extra reviews
Ignore it because accuracy is unchanged
Widen immediately to collect more data
Guardrails exist for costs like manual review; investigate before widening.
At 5% for 12 hours, a canary shows 90.2% against 94.1% for control, p < 0.001. What is the right decision?
Extend the bake to a week
The drop is large and statistically clear, so the guardrail says roll back.
The canary’s success equals control’s after a well-sized stage. What is the right next step?
Promote to the next stage and bake again
Stop the experiment and keep 5% forever
Switch the control group to the canary
No detectable harm at the right sample size is the signal to widen.
A bank’s prompt canary covers weekday mornings only. Why can that give a false picture? Select all that apply.
Traffic mix differs on evenings and weekends
Some problems appear only for request types that are rare in the morning
Morning users are always more accurate
Canaries must never run in the morning
Bake long enough to cover the daily and weekly traffic mix.
A canary is run for a new model snapshot rather than a prompt. What should the flag control?
The snapshot name in the release used for that user
The flag selects which release, including the snapshot, serves each user.
Which of these can a canary catch that offline evals may miss? Select all that apply.
Behaviour on real inputs that the test set never covered
Latency and cost under real load
Syntax errors in the prompt template file
A model alias moved by the provider last month
Live traffic reveals real inputs and load; template syntax fails earlier, and provider moves are not your release.
onlineeval: A homework-help agent answers 40,000 questions a day, evenly spread. A judge scores 1% of them. How many judged answers fall in a 12-hour window?
In that setup, each judgement costs ₹0.50. What does judging cost per day?
A window has 400 judged answers with a 90% pass rate. Roughly what is the standard error of the pass rate?
Offline evals pass, but claims staff report worse summaries. Which is the most useful next step?
Score a sample of live traffic and compare it with the baseline
The offline suite may not reflect today’s inputs; live scoring shows what users actually get.
Which checks are cheap enough to run on every production answer? Select all that apply.
A required citation marker is present
Deterministic checks cost almost nothing; judges and humans are for samples.
An alert on a 15-minute window fires several times a week with nothing wrong. What is the most likely cause?
The window holds too few judgements, so noise crosses the threshold
Small samples have large standard errors; widen the window or require a minimum sample.
The intent mix moves from {returns 60%, orders 40%} to {returns 40%, orders 60%}. Using PSI = Σ (actual − expected) × ln(actual ÷ expected), roughly what is the PSI?
Each term is 0.2 × ln(1.5) ≈ 0.081, so PSI ≈ 0.16: a moderate shift.
A common rule of thumb reads PSI above which value as a significant distribution shift?
Under 0.1 is usually stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 significant.
A health-information agent’s judge is being set up for online scoring. What should be true before its scores drive alerts? Select all that apply.
It has been calibrated against human labels
Its sample is random, not hand-picked
It uses the same model as the agent
A calibrated judge on a random sample gives unbiased, trustworthy estimates.
Why alert on scores per important segment, such as intent or language, and not only on the global average?
A failing segment can hide inside a healthy average
A 20-point drop in a 10% segment moves the average only 2 points.
An online eval confirms that a set of claim types now fails. What should happen to those cases?
Add them to the offline eval suite
Ignore them once the alert clears
Failing live cases make the offline suite more representative for the next release.
A brokerage wants faster detection without more false alerts. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
Judge a larger sample, so each window is more precise
Use a window long enough for a stable estimate but short enough to react
Alert on every single failed answer
More judgements and a well-chosen window reduce noise; tiny thresholds and per-answer alerts increase it.
With a 24-hour window and an 8-point threshold, false alerts vanish, but a real 6-point drop takes days to catch. Why?
The threshold is larger than the drop, so each window rarely crosses it
A threshold above the true drop means only noisy windows cross it, so detection is slow.
What does an online eval add that user thumbs-down signals alone do not?
A consistent, unbiased quality estimate, since few users click and those who do are not typical
Feedback is sparse and self-selected; a sampled judge measures quality systematically.
Which belong in an alert rule for online evals? Select all that apply.
A threshold relative to baseline and a minimum sample size
Metric, window, threshold and minimum sample define when a page is justified.
A logistics agent’s judge pass rate is steady, but PSI on request types jumps to 0.31 after a new customer onboards. What is the best reading?
Nothing to act on because scores are fine
Inputs have shifted significantly; check quality on the new request types before it shows in the average
Drift often precedes a quality drop on the new kinds of request.
A support team judges 100% of traffic with an LLM judge. What is the main downside?
The cost scales with all traffic, when a random sample would estimate quality almost as well
It removes the need for a baseline
Sampling gives nearly the same estimate at a small fraction of the cost.
Which could explain a drop in live quality while offline evals still pass? Select all that apply.
Users started asking kinds of questions missing from the test set
The provider changed the snapshot behind an alias
The offline suite ran after the change and caught it
New inputs and silent model changes both escape a fixed, earlier offline run.
Where should an online-eval page link to, so triage starts fast?
The failing traces behind the drop
Linking to failing examples lets the engineer see what broke immediately.
Which settings reduce judge cost without making the alert blind? Select all that apply.
Sample a fixed percentage chosen for enough judgements per window
Run cheap deterministic checks on everything and the judge only on a sample
Judge only answers that users already liked
A sized sample plus cheap checks keeps cost low and coverage honest; biased or gapped sampling does not.
durable: A cashless-claim job waits up to two days for a surveyor. What is the problem with a Python process that sleeps while waiting?
Any restart or deploy in those two days loses the wait and the progress
Python cannot sleep for two days
The surveyor cannot see the claim
A durable signal or timer survives restarts; a sleeping process does not.
An 8-step loan job crashes during step 6. A plain script restarts from step 1. Steps 2, 3 and 4 are model calls of 5,000 tokens each. How many tokens of completed work are wasted?
Completed model steps 2, 3 and 4 run again: 3 × 5,000 = 15,000.
