A Temporal activity releases a payment. The worker crashes after the bank accepted it but before the result was recorded. What happens next?
The activity may run again, so the payment needs an idempotency key
Activities are at least once; the key makes the retry return the first result.
Which code must go in activities rather than in Temporal workflow code?
Model calls, API calls and anything else with I/O
Loops over a list already in memory
Workflow code is replayed; I/O runs in activities, whose results are recorded.
Which of these make Temporal workflow code non-deterministic? Select all that apply.
Awaiting execute_activity for a model call
Wall-clock time and random numbers differ on replay; activities and the workflow clock are deterministic.
The recorded sequence of a workflow’s events, including each completed activity’s result
Replaying the history rebuilds the workflow’s state after a crash.
A LangGraph agent uses a Postgres checkpointer. After a pod restart, how does it continue a paused run?
It restarts automatically on its own
It is invoked again with the same thread id and loads the saved state
Checkpointers save state per thread; something must call the graph again with that thread id.
A claims job crashes during the payment step. Which combination avoids both a double payment and asking the surveyor again? Select all that apply.
Resume from recorded state instead of restarting from step 1
Send an idempotency key with the payment
Restart the whole job from step 1
Recorded state keeps the approval; the key makes the repeated payment safe.
A returns-processing agent finishes in 3 seconds and has no side effects. Is durable execution worth it?
Probably not: a failed request can simply be retried
Yes, because it makes the model faster
No, because it cannot call models
Durable execution pays off for long, costly or side-effecting work.
What does a RetryPolicy with maximum_attempts=4 on a model-call activity give you?
Four different answers to choose from
Up to four attempts, with backoff, before the activity fails
Transient failures are retried by the engine, not by hand-written loops.
A workflow waits for a customer to upload documents, with a deadline of 7 days. Which Temporal features fit?
A signal for the upload and a durable timer for the deadline
A while loop that polls every second
A cron job that restarts the workflow
Signals deliver events and timers enforce deadlines, both durably.
Which are true of activities in Temporal? Select all that apply.
They can be retried according to a policy
Activities are where I/O belongs, with timeouts and retries; they are at least once, not exactly once.
A team changes the order of steps in a running workflow’s code. Why can this break in-flight workflows?
Replay of existing histories no longer matches the new code
Workflow code changes need versioning so old executions replay with the old logic.
A 10-step job crashes during step 7. Under a durable workflow, how many steps run again?
Steps 1 to 6 come from history; only the step in flight, 7, runs again.
When is a LangGraph checkpointer usually enough, rather than a full durable engine? Select all that apply.
The agent pauses for a human and is resumed by the next user request
Losing a few seconds of in-flight work is acceptable
Workflows run for weeks with many timers and side effects
Resumption must happen automatically within seconds after any crash
Checkpointers suit request-driven pauses; long, timer-heavy, auto-resuming workflows suit engines like Temporal.
What is the main purpose of the idempotency key in f"pay-{claim_id}"?
To make repeated payment calls for the same claim return the first result
The same key on a retry lets the receiving API deduplicate it.
Why is durable execution valuable for expensive model steps even without side effects?
It makes model calls cheaper per token
Completed steps are not recomputed after a crash, so their tokens are not spent twice
It removes the need for timeouts
Recorded results replace recomputation on resume.
A loan-origination workflow calls a credit bureau, waits for a committee, then disburses. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
Bureau call as an activity with a timeout and retries
The committee wait as a sleeping thread
Reading the clock directly in workflow code
Activities with timeouts and keyed side effects are sound; sleeping threads and wall-clock reads in workflow code are not.
A rebooking workflow’s worker is redeployed mid-run. What happens under Temporal?
Another worker picks up the workflow and replays its history
The server pauses until the same worker returns
Any worker on the task queue can continue the workflow from its history.
Which statement best contrasts durable execution with idempotency (Tools & MCP)?
Durable execution resumes the workflow; idempotency makes each repeated side effect safe
Durable execution makes idempotency keys unnecessary
You need both: resumption for progress, keys for safe repeats.
resilience: An order-support assistant receives 50 requests a second, each taking 4 s on average. By Little’s law, how many are in flight at once?
A service has a pool of 300 workers and 30 requests a second. What is the highest average request time it can sustain?
300 ÷ 30 = 10 s; any longer and requests queue.
The Anthropic and OpenAI Python SDKs, left at defaults, time out after how long?
Both default to 10 minutes, far longer than most user-facing targets.
Three layers each retry a failed call twice, three attempts per layer. In the worst case, how many attempts reach the provider for one user request?
Which belong in a safe retry policy? Select all that apply.
A small retry budget as a share of traffic
Retrying every error immediately in a tight loop
Backoff, jitter and budgets limit load; immediate retries and retrying bad requests add it.
What does a circuit breaker do after the failure threshold is reached?
Opens and fails fast without calling the dependency, then probes after a cooldown
Open means skip the dependency; half-open lets a probe test recovery.
In the half-open state, a probe call succeeds. What happens?
The breaker closes and normal calls resume
All requests go to the fallback
A successful probe closes the breaker.
Primary calls fail 40% of the time during an outage. With 2 retries (3 attempts) and independent failures, what share of requests fail every attempt?
0.4³ = 0.064, so 6.4% still fail after three attempts.
During a provider outage, which changes lower p95 latency for users? Select all that apply.
A circuit breaker that skips the failing provider
More retries on the failing provider
Skipping the failure and bounding waits cut latency; retries and long timeouts add to it.
A symptom-checker falls back to a smaller model during outages. What must be true before relying on it?
The fallback has been evaluated on the task and exercised in drills
It must be from the same provider
It must be larger than the primary
Untested fallbacks answer differently and may fail on the day they are needed.
What is a bulkhead in resilience design?
A separate concurrency limit per dependency, so one slow dependency cannot use every worker
Bulkheads isolate failures by capping resources per dependency.
At market open a provider slows down and the whole order assistant goes down. Which are likely contributing causes? Select all that apply.
Retries multiplied load on the struggling provider
Long waits exhaust workers and retries amplify load; prompt length and batch export are not causes.
A 3-second timeout cuts off 10% of healthy calls that take a little longer. What is the trade-off?
No trade-off; shorter is always better
Shorter timeouts free workers faster but turn slow successes into failures
Set timeouts from the latency distribution of healthy calls, not as low as possible.
When both the primary and the secondary provider fail, what should a customer-facing agent return?
A cached answer or a clear message about the delay
A graceful last resort beats an error page or a hung request.
Which tools provide cross-provider fallbacks for model calls? Select all that apply.
LiteLLM and Portkey route between providers with fallbacks; the others handle drift and prompt versions.
In LiteLLM’s Router, what does a cooldown do?
Takes a deployment that keeps failing out of rotation for a period
Failing deployments are skipped for the cooldown time, similar to an open breaker.
A pybreaker breaker is configured with fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30. What does this mean?
Open after 5 consecutive failures and try again after 30 seconds
fail_max is the failure threshold; reset_timeout is the cooldown before a probe.
An outage drill injects 40% errors into the primary provider. What should the team measure? Select all that apply.
Drills check whether users still get good, timely answers and whether capacity holds.
Why should a retried payment tool call carry an idempotency key even behind a circuit breaker?
A timed-out call may still have succeeded, so a retry could pay twice
Timeouts do not mean failure on the other side; keys make retries safe.
Which designs keep an assistant up when its only model provider degrades? Select all that apply.
Short timeouts and a small retry budget
A circuit breaker with a tested fallback
More workers with the same 10-minute timeout
Retrying every failed call five times
Bounded waits and fail-fast fallbacks protect capacity; more workers and more retries only delay the collapse.
incident: A payments company’s refund agent starts paying some refunds twice right after a prompt change. Money is still leaving. What should the on-call engineer do first?
Edit the prompt live to forbid repeat refunds
Turn off the refund tool with a kill switch, then roll back to the last good release
Read the logs until the root cause is clear
Contain before you diagnose. A kill switch and a rollback to a tested release stop the harm without guessing under pressure.
Duplicate refunds leak ₹1,000 a minute. An alert detects the problem after 12 minutes and the kill switch stops it 5 minutes later. How much is lost?
The same leak of ₹1,000 a minute is found through merchant complaints after 240 minutes instead of an alert after 12, with the same 5-minute kill switch. How much more is lost?
A marketplace alerts when the refund rate in a 10-minute window exceeds 1.5 times its 2.1% baseline, with at least 500 orders. A window has 900 orders and 40 refunds. What happens?
No alert: 40 refunds is a small number
No alert: the window is too small
The alert fires: 4.4% is above the 3.15% threshold
The alert fires only if complaints arrive too
1.5 × 2.1% = 3.15%, and 40 ÷ 900 = 4.4%, with 900 orders above the 500 minimum.
A bank’s engineer re-runs a failing loan-support request against today’s live systems, and the agent behaves correctly. Why is that not proof the bug is gone?
The tools now return different data than at the time of failure, so the conditions were not reproduced
The model has been retrained overnight
Re-runs are always correct by design
A faithful reproduction needs the original input, release and recorded tool responses; live data has moved on.
What must a trace hold so that a failing agent run can be replayed deterministically? Select all that apply.
The release: prompt version, model snapshot and parameters
Every tool call with its recorded response
Input, release and recorded tool responses let the run be repeated offline without touching live systems.
An insurer replays a failing claims trace, but the replay harness calls the live policy and payout APIs. What is the main danger?
A replay can trigger real payouts and sees different data, so it is neither safe nor faithful
Replays must serve recorded responses, never call systems with side effects.
A telecom support agent begins granting unauthorised plan credits after a model snapshot update. The quickest containment that keeps the rest of the agent working is:
Shut down the whole support website
Disable only the credit tool with a flag, and pin the previous snapshot
Ask customers to stop requesting credits
Disabling one tool limits harm while the agent still answers questions; pinning the old snapshot restores the last good release.
A hotfix goes live 40 minutes after detection and stops 75% of a ₹60,000-an-hour leak. The rest continues for 20 more hours. How much does the residual leak cost?
25% of ₹60,000 is ₹15,000 an hour; over 20 hours that is ₹3,00,000.
Which signals are good automated detectors for a misbehaving production agent? Select all that apply.
A drop in the sampled judge score on live traffic
A spike in tool error rates
A business-metric anomaly such as refund rate per order
Quality scores, tool errors and business metrics detect problems early; user reports remain a backstop.
After an incident, a hospital’s post-mortem draft says “Dr Rao’s team shipped a bad prompt”. What should a blameless post-mortem ask instead?
Why the system allowed an untested prompt to reach production, and what will stop it next time
Whether the prompt was long enough
Blameless reviews look for system causes and owned actions; blame hides information and repeats failures.
A SEBI-registered broker’s order-help agent gives wrong margin figures. Which severity fits best if customers are placing trades on those figures right now?
SEV1: harm is happening now, page immediately
SEV3: fix in the next sprint
SEV2 only if the press notices
Active harm to customers’ money calls for the top severity, a single owner and immediate containment.
An incident that falls under CERT-In’s reporting directions is noticed at 22:30. By when must it be reported, under the 6-hour rule?
Six hours after 22:30 is 04:30. Whether a given incident is reportable is for your compliance team; this is educational, not legal advice.
Which items belong in a blameless post-mortem? Select all that apply.
A timeline from first signal to full recovery
Impact, such as orders affected and rupees lost
Actions, each with an owner and a date
All four make the review useful: what happened, how bad, why, and what changes, owned by someone.
An NBFC fixes an incident where its collections agent sent messages at night, but adds no test. Three months later a new prompt brings the bug back. What was missing?
An eval case built from the failing trace, run in the release gate
Turning the failure into an eval case means any future release that repeats it fails before shipping.
A kill-switch flag is read once when the service starts and stored in a variable. During an incident the flag is flipped off. What happens?
Nothing changes until the processes restart
The flag provider restarts the service
The model stops calling the tool
A kill switch must be read on every call, or flipping it has no effect on running processes.
A claims agent’s bad behaviour began when the prompt and the model snapshot changed together in release rel-v12. What should the rollback restore?
The whole previous release: prompt, snapshot, tools and parameters
Roll back to a known-good combination; mixing an old prompt with a new model is a release nobody tested.
During a SEV1, what should the incident commander do? Select all that apply.
Decide on containment and assign investigators
Post status updates on a fixed rhythm
Check with compliance whether any reporting duty applies
The commander coordinates, communicates and brings in compliance; hands-on debugging is delegated.
A replay of trace tr-4f91 under prompt v8 calls issue_refund twice in 10 of 10 runs; under v7 it calls it once. What does that establish?
The failure is random and cannot be fixed
v8 causes the double refund under the recorded conditions, so the case can become a regression test
The payment gateway is at fault
A consistent reproduction pins the cause to the release change and gives you a ready-made eval case.
A health app stores full traces for replay, including patients’ messages and tool responses. What must go with that?
Redaction of personal data, access control and a retention limit, as DPDP-style obligations expect
Replayable traces are valuable and sensitive; redact, restrict and expire them.
feedback: Why are thumbs ratings alone not enough?
Few users rate and they skew to extremes
Which are implicit signals? Select all that apply.
What must each signal be linked to?
The trace, prompt version and context
Named failure patterns with counts and owners
A fix for a pattern should ship when?
Under DPDP, training on chat logs needs?
A lawful basis such as notice and consent, plus redaction
How much users change the assistant’s output
Resolution rises from 72% to 79%. On 2 lakh chats, how many more resolved a week?
Which technique scores sampled traffic automatically?
This one is about user signals.
Which make a flywheel turn? Select all that apply.
Fixes are measured on the eval set
Pattern-to-fix time falls from 45 to 10 days. Days saved?
A handoff to a human after the assistant answered usually signals?
Why cluster rather than read every negative trace?
Volume is too high; patterns show what matters most
Implicit signals are noisy. What reduces the noise?
Combining several signals and reviewing samples
What should a triage record per pattern? Select all that apply.
Top 5 patterns × 20 eval cases each adds?
Feedback collected but never reviewed results in?
Which is a good weekly triage sample size for one reviewer?

tracing.q: Success dropped overnight with no deploy. Walk through how you would use traces to find the cause.
tracing.model: Pull the failed traces from the window since the drop and group them by each attribute in turn: prompt version, tool, region, and the served model, gen_ai.response.model. Dimensions whose groups all sit at the same rate are not the cause. Here the served model splits cleanly: the old snapshot still succeeds, the new one does not, and it now serves most traffic, which means the provider moved the alias. Confirm on a few examples, pin the old snapshot, and watch the success rate recover.

tracing.q: What would you capture on spans, and what would you deliberately leave out? Why?
tracing.model: Capture the operation and provider, the requested and served model, token usage, finish reason, timings and error status on every span, plus your own release id. Leave full prompt and completion text off by default, because it can contain personal data; enable it only where needed, with redaction, access control and a retention limit. Keep every error trace and sample successful ones to control cost.

tracing.q: How do traces connect to evaluation (Evaluation) and cost control (Cost Optimisation)?
pts: tokens per step drive cost work
tracing.model: Traces are the raw material for both. Process-level evaluation grades the steps of a run, and those steps are the spans; failing live traces become new cases in the offline suite. Token counts per span show which steps and tools drive spend, which tells you where step caps, pruning or a smaller model will save the most.

versioning.q: Design the release record for an agent. What goes in it, and how is it used during an incident?
versioning.model: A release bundles the prompt name and version, the pinned model snapshot, the tool definitions and their versions, and generation parameters, hashed into one id that is stamped on every trace. During an incident you filter traces by release to see whether failures started with a new one; if so, you move the production label back to the previous version, with no redeploy.

versioning.q: Why pin model snapshots, and what new work does pinning create?
pts: pinned only changes when you choose
versioning.model: An alias can be pointed at a new snapshot by the provider, so your behaviour can change without a deploy. A pinned snapshot changes only when you change it. The cost is that snapshots are retired on a published schedule, so you must track deprecation dates and plan migrations: evaluate the new snapshot offline, canary it on live traffic, then promote it.

versioning.q: Several teams edit prompts. How do you keep speed without losing control?
versioning.model: Put prompts in a registry where every edit creates a version, and let anyone propose a version. Promotion is gated: a reviewer approves, the offline evals must pass, and only then does the staging label move, followed by a canary and the production label. Each team moves fast on drafts, while production changes stay reviewed, tested and reversible.

canary.q: How do you decide the size and duration of a canary stage?
canary.model: Start from the smallest drop you must not miss, say 4 points from 94%, and compute the sample needed for about 80% power: roughly 350 canary conversations for a one-sided test. Divide by the canary’s share of traffic to get the bake time, and extend it to cover the daily traffic mix. Small gains need far larger samples than large drops.

canary.q: What can go wrong in the plumbing of a prompt canary, and how do you prevent it?
canary.model: Assignment must be sticky, by hashing a stable user id, or conversations mix versions. The variant must be recorded on every trace and metric, or you cannot compare the groups. And the comparison must be against a concurrent control, not last week’s numbers, because traffic mix changes by hour and day.

canary.q: When is a canary the wrong tool?
canary.model: With very low traffic a canary never reaches a meaningful sample, so rely on offline evals and careful manual review. When a change must reach everyone at once, such as a regulatory or security fix, ship it with monitoring and a rollback ready. And a canary only guards your own releases; it cannot catch a change the provider makes behind an alias, which is why snapshots are pinned.

onlineeval.q: Design an online eval and alert for a support agent. Name the numbers you would set.
pts: checks on all, judge on sample
onlineeval.model: Run cheap checks such as format, citation and PII on every answer, and a calibrated judge on a random 1–5%. Aggregate in windows of a few hours with a minimum number of judgements, and set the threshold from the metric’s normal variation, a few standard errors below baseline, so false alerts are rare. Page with links to failing traces, and add confirmed failures to the offline suite.

onlineeval.q: Offline evals passed and users still say quality dropped. What could explain it, and how do online evals help?
onlineeval.model: The offline set is fixed and may not reflect today’s inputs: users may be asking new kinds of questions, or the provider may have changed the model. Online evals score what users actually send, so they show the drop, and drift metrics such as PSI on intents show whether the inputs themselves moved. Failing live cases then extend the offline set so it stays representative.

onlineeval.q: How do you keep online judging affordable and trustworthy?
onlineeval.model: Judge a random sample rather than everything, sized so each window has enough judgements to be stable. Calibrate the judge against human labels before trusting it, and re-check that agreement periodically. Break scores down by important segments such as intent or language, because a failing segment can hide inside a healthy average.

durable.q: Explain what durable execution guarantees, and what it does not.
durable.model: A durable engine records the result of every completed step in an event history, so after a crash or redeploy the workflow replays that history and continues from the step in flight, and it can wait for days without a live process. It does not make side effects exactly once: an activity can run again if the worker dies after the effect but before the result is recorded, so payments, emails and tickets still need idempotency keys.

durable.q: When is a LangGraph checkpointer enough, and when would you choose Temporal?
durable.model: A checkpointer saves the graph’s state after each step, keyed by thread id, which is enough for agents that pause for a human and can be resumed by the next request or a supervisor job. Choose a durable engine such as Temporal when workflows run for days, involve many side effects and retries, must resume automatically after any crash, and need timers and an audit history.

durable.q: Why must workflow code be deterministic, and how do you keep it that way?
durable.model: After a crash, the worker re-executes the workflow code against the recorded history to rebuild state, so the code must make the same decisions it made the first time. Keep clocks, random numbers and all I/O out of workflow code: use the engine’s deterministic time and timers, and do network calls, model calls and anything non-deterministic in activities, whose results are recorded.

resilience.q: A provider slows down and your whole service goes down. Explain why, using Little’s law, and how to prevent it.
resilience.model: Requests in flight equal the arrival rate times the time each one takes. When calls hang until a 10-minute default timeout, time per request explodes, so in-flight requests exceed the worker pool and even healthy requests are rejected. Short timeouts bound the time, a circuit breaker stops sending traffic to the failing provider, and a fallback turns failures into fast answers.

resilience.q: How can retries make an outage worse, and what is a safe retry policy?
resilience.model: Every retry is another request to a dependency that is already struggling, and retries at several layers multiply the load into a retry storm. A safe policy retries only retryable errors, a small number of times, with exponential backoff and jitter, within a retry budget as a share of traffic, and relies on a circuit breaker to stop calling a dependency whose failures persist.

A fallback model answers differently, so evaluate it on your own task before you rely on it. Exercise it regularly in drills that inject latency and errors, so the path actually works on the day it is needed. And tag and monitor fallback traffic separately, so you can see how often it runs and whether its quality holds.

incident.q: A refund agent starts paying some refunds twice right after a prompt change. Walk through your incident response, from the first alert to the post-mortem.
pts: replay the trace for the root cause
incident.model: An alert on the refund rate pages the on-call engineer, who declares a SEV1 with one incident commander, because money is leaving every minute. Containment comes before diagnosis: a flag turns off the refund tool so refunds queue for people, and the release, prompt and model together, rolls back to the last good version. Then the failing trace is replayed offline with the same input, release and recorded tool responses until the double refund reproduces and the root cause is clear. The trace becomes an eval case in the release gate, the fix ships through that gate, and a blameless post-mortem records the timeline, impact, causes and owned actions.

incident.q: Duplicate refunds cost ₹1,000 a minute. Complaints take 240 minutes to surface the problem and an alert takes 12. A live hotfix takes 40 minutes and stops 75% of the leak for the rest of the day; a kill switch takes 5 minutes and stops all of it. Compare complaints with a hotfix against an alert with a kill switch over a 1,440-minute day. Show the working.
incident.model: Alert and kill switch: (12 + 5) = 17 minutes × ₹1,000 = ₹17,000. Complaints and hotfix: the full leak runs 240 + 40 = 280 minutes, ₹2,80,000; then 25% keeps leaking, ₹250 a minute, for 1,440 − 280 = 1,160 minutes, ₹2,90,000. Total ₹5,70,000, more than 33 times the loss.

incident.q: Your team is at an Indian payments company. During the incident someone asks whether you must tell a regulator, and later the post-mortem draft names the engineer who shipped v8 as the cause. How do you handle both?
pts: CERT-In 6 hours for specified cyber incidents
incident.model: Bring compliance in early rather than deciding alone. CERT-In’s 2022 directions require specified cyber security incidents to be reported within 6 hours of noticing them, and RBI-regulated entities have their own incident-reporting expectations; a prompt bug that causes duplicate refunds may or may not fall under these, while a data leak or unauthorised access likely would, so the compliance team makes the call. This is educational context, not legal advice. For the post-mortem, remove the name: ask why the system let an untested instruction reach production and pay twice. The actions are systemic, each with an owner: an eval case in the release gate, an idempotency key on refunds, a canary for prompt changes and a refund-rate alert.

feedback.q: How would you build a feedback loop for a support assistant?
feedback.model: Log thumbs plus implicit signals such as retries, rephrasing and handoffs on each trace; triage a weekly sample into named failure patterns with owners; turn each into eval cases and a fix; add consented, redacted examples to training data; measure each release.

feedback.q: 2 lakh chats, 1.5% rated, 20% negative. Thumbs-down a week?
The team has 50,000 thumbs-down rows and no idea what to do with them. Advice?
feedback.model: Sample a few hundred with their traces, cluster them into named patterns with counts, give the top few owners, and turn each into eval cases that a fix must pass; repeat weekly.

cases.tag: A change you did not make
cases.title: The copilot that got worse overnight
cases.brief: A general insurer's health-claims copilot summarises claims for 400 desk staff. Last Tuesday the share of summaries accepted without edits fell from 94% to 86% overnight. It took two days to find the cause: the provider had moved the model alias the config points at. The head of the claims desk wants a plan so the next incident is caught in hours rather than days.
evidence: There was no deploy that night. The configuration names the model alias alpha-latest, and the prompt is a string in the application code.
Logs are one plain-text line per request: no spans, no token counts, and no record of which model snapshot served each call.
The offline eval suite still passes. It last ran a week ago, before the change.
Last month a provider slowdown pushed p95 latency to 40 s for ten minutes. The service stayed up, but the desk complained.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.tracing: Start here, because the brief's actual request is to shorten two days to hours, and two days is what you get from one plain-text line per request. Spans per step, token counts, and - the specific omission that cost this team two days - the model snapshot that served each call. Record the snapshot the provider actually used, not the alias you asked for, keep every failed trace while sampling the successful ones, and redact personal data before it reaches the tracing backend.
why.versioning: An alias in the config is a standing invitation for the provider to change your model without a deploy, and that is precisely what happened. Pin the snapshot, treat the prompt as a reviewed, versioned artefact rather than a string in the code, and put the retirement date of the snapshot in the calendar so pinning does not become its own outage next year.
why.onlineeval: An offline suite that passes and last ran a week ago cannot see a change that happened on Tuesday night - and it never will, because the inputs and the dependency move while the suite stands still. Score live traffic continuously, alert per segment rather than on the average, use a window wide enough not to fire on noise, and calibrate the judge against human labels.
why.resilience: Useful, and it is the one piece of unfinished business from last month: a provider slowdown taking p95 to 40 s means the default timeout is far too generous. Set timeouts from your own latency target, give retries a budget, add a circuit breaker, and test the fallback path before the day it is needed.
why.incident: Useful as the discipline wrapped around all of this: once traces include tool responses you can replay a bad run, and the post-mortem should add a test rather than name a person. It depends on the tracing work, so it follows rather than leads.
why.canary: Not needed for this incident, and it is the instructive exclusion: a canary protects you from changes you ship, and there was no deploy that night. It will matter for your own prompt and model upgrades - including the pinned snapshot you are about to move to - but it could not have caught this.
why.durable: Not needed: summarising one claim is a single short request with no human approval in the middle and no side effects to replay. Nothing here runs long enough to lose progress.
why.feedback: Not needed as a new build: the accept-without-edits rate is already a good implicit signal and it did detect the drop. The failure was not in collecting feedback, it was in nobody watching it continuously or being able to explain it.

firstWhy.versioning: The cause of this incident and your second step, so this is the strongest wrong answer here. Pinning the snapshot stops this exact recurrence - but the request was to catch the next incident in hours, and the next one will have a different cause. Two days of diagnosis came from having no spans and no record of what served each call.
firstWhy.onlineeval: Right that an offline suite run weekly cannot catch an overnight change, and live scoring is what turns days into hours of detection. But an alert tells you quality dropped; it does not tell you why, and without per-step traces carrying the model snapshot you are back to two days of hunting with a faster start.
firstWhy.resilience: A real gap and the desk already complained about it, so fix it this quarter. But it addresses last month's incident rather than this one, and nothing in it would shorten the diagnosis of a silent quality change.

cases.model: Start with tracing, because the explicit ask is to turn two days of diagnosis into hours and one plain-text line per request is why it took two days: emit spans per step with token counts and, critically, the model snapshot that actually served each call rather than the alias you requested - that single field is what was missing. Keep every failed trace, sample the successful ones, and redact personal data before it reaches the backend. Then fix versioning: pin the snapshot instead of pointing at alpha-latest, move the prompt out of application code into a reviewed, versioned artefact with an eval gate, and diary the snapshot's retirement date. Next add online evals with drift alerts, since an offline suite that last ran a week ago can never see a Tuesday-night change - score live traffic, alert per segment rather than on averages, use a stable window, and calibrate the judge against human labels. Then finish last month's business with timeouts set from your own target, a retry budget, a circuit breaker and a tested fallback. Wrap it in incident practice that replays traces and adds tests. A canary could not have caught this because nobody deployed anything; there is no long-running task to checkpoint; and the accept-without-edits signal you already have worked.
cases.note: The cause was the alias and the fix is to pin it, and still the first move is observability - because the brief asked to catch the next incident, not to re-fight this one. Case 3 is a regression the team shipped itself, where the ordering goes the other way.

tracing: The brief asks for the next incident to be caught in hours rather than days. Symptom 2 explains the days: one plain-text line per request, no spans, no token counts, and no record of which model snapshot served each call. What is missing?
Structured, per-step records of what ran - including which model actually answered, rather than which one you asked for. There is a sampling rule and a privacy rule worth noting too.
OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing. The first pitfall - logging only the requested model hides a silent provider-side change - is this entire incident.
versioning: Symptom 1: no deploy happened, the config names the alias alpha-latest, and the prompt is a string in the code. Who changed the system?
Someone outside your company, because you asked for “latest”. And one of your two most important artefacts is not under review at all.
Prompt and Model Versioning. Read the pitfall about an alias letting the provider change your model without a deploy, and the one about pinning forever and missing a retirement date.
onlineeval: Symptom 3: the offline eval suite still passes, and it last ran a week ago - before the change. What can an offline suite, run weekly, never tell you?
Whether quality is slipping on live traffic right now. Note how the window, the judge and the choice of what to average over decide whether such alerts are useful or ignored.
Online Evals and Drift Alerts. Read the pitfalls about a window too small, an uncalibrated judge, and alerting on averages that hide a failing segment.

drop.canary: A canary release ships a change to a slice of traffic before all of it. Read symptom 1 again: what deploy was there that night?
drop.durable: Durable execution checkpoints long tasks so a crash does not lose progress. How long does summarising one claim take, and what side effects does it have?
drop.feedback: Feedback loops turn user signals into an eval set. What signal does this team already have - and did it detect the drop?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now re-read what the head of the claims desk actually asked for: not that this cause never recurs, but that the next incident is caught in hours. Which of your choices shortens a diagnosis you have not had yet?

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A model alias let the provider change the model with no deploy, which is the direct cause of this incident.
The offline suite runs weekly and could never have detected an overnight change in live quality.
With no spans and no record of which snapshot served each call, any incident takes days to diagnose - and the ask was to make the next one hours.
whyFirst.why: Order by the brief you were given. Pinning the snapshot prevents this recurrence and must happen, and online evals are what shorten detection - but the request was about the next incident, whose cause will be something else. What turned a Tuesday-night change into a two-day hunt was that nothing recorded which model answered which call, and that gap makes every future incident expensive too.

cases.title: The refund workflow that paid twice after a deploy
cases.brief: A marketplace runs an agent that investigates refund requests, waits for a human approval above a threshold, then issues the payment and notifies the merchant. Runs take twenty minutes to three days because of the approval wait. Quality is not in question - nobody has complained about the agent's judgement. What they complain about is what happens when something restarts.
evidence: A run's state lives in process memory. A routine Tuesday deploy lost 180 in-flight runs, and the merchants waiting on them were never told.
After one crash the payment step ran a second time: the team had assumed exactly-once delivery. Twenty-three merchants were refunded twice.
The workflow code calls datetime.now() and makes random choices inline, so a replay takes a different path than the original run.
Provider calls use the default ten-minute timeout. During one slowdown, hung calls exhausted every worker and the queue stopped entirely. Retries have no budget.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.durable: Start here, and it covers the two most expensive symptoms. State in process memory is why a routine deploy destroyed 180 in-flight runs; assuming exactly-once is why a crash paid 23 merchants twice. Persist the workflow and checkpoint at every step rather than at the end, make every side-effecting activity idempotent so a replay cannot repeat the payment, and move datetime.now() and random choices out of the workflow body - non-deterministic workflow code is what makes replay take a different path, which is symptom 3 precisely.
why.resilience: A default ten-minute timeout on a user-facing path is how one provider slowdown stopped the entire queue, and retries without a budget are how you turn a slowdown into an outage. Set timeouts from your own target, budget the retries, add a circuit breaker so a failing dependency is shed rather than queued against, and test the fallback before you need it.
why.incident: Traces that hold prompts but not tool responses cannot be replayed - a live re-run sees different data and the bug will not reproduce - and someone hot-fixed a prompt in production while refunds were still going out, which is the named worst practice. Capture tool responses, replay rather than re-run, stop the money before editing anything, and end each post-mortem with a test instead of a name.
why.tracing: Useful and the foundation for the above: spans per step with token counts and recorded tool responses. Secondary because the immediate failures are structural rather than diagnostic - you know exactly what went wrong here.
why.versioning: Useful: refund decisions are auditable work, so pinning the model snapshot and versioning prompts matters for explaining a past decision. No symptom here was caused by a version change, so it is hygiene rather than a fix.
why.canary: Not needed: nothing in this evidence was caused by a change the team shipped. A canary limits the blast radius of your own releases, and the blast radius here came from crashes and timeouts.
why.onlineeval: Not needed on this evidence: nobody has questioned the agent's judgement, and no symptom describes quality drifting. Every failure is about execution, not about the answer.
why.feedback: Not needed: the merchants reported this loudly and immediately. There is no detection gap to close with a feedback loop.

firstWhy.resilience: Important and your second step - a ten-minute default timeout that lets hung calls exhaust every worker is indefensible, and it stopped the whole queue once already. But that outage ended; the double refunds did not un-happen, and the next deploy will drop another 180 runs on the floor. Fix what loses money and work permanently, then stop the dependency taking you down.
firstWhy.incident: The sharpest observation on the page - traces without tool responses cannot reproduce anything, and hot-fixing a prompt while refunds are still going out is exactly wrong. But incident practice is how you handle the next failure well, and two of these failures are structural: they will keep happening on every crash and every deploy until the execution model changes.
firstWhy.tracing: The right foundation and you will need it for the replay work. But you are not short of diagnosis here - you know the runs were in memory, you know the payment ran twice, you know the timeout was ten minutes. Spend the first move on the cause, not on seeing it more clearly.

cases.model: Start with durable execution and checkpointing, because it answers the two failures that cost money and work: persist run state instead of holding it in process memory, so a deploy cannot destroy 180 in-flight runs, and checkpoint every step rather than only at the end. Make every side-effecting activity idempotent, because exactly-once does not exist and an activity can run again after a crash - that is why 23 merchants were refunded twice. Move datetime.now() and random choices out of the workflow body, since non-deterministic workflow code is exactly why replay takes a different path. Then fix resilience: timeouts derived from your own target rather than a ten-minute default, a retry budget, a circuit breaker so a slow provider is shed instead of queued against, and a fallback path that has actually been tested. Next build real incident practice - capture tool responses in traces so a bad run can be replayed rather than re-run against different data, halt the money before touching a prompt, and close every post-mortem with a test. Tracing and versioning are the supporting hygiene. Canaries, online evals and feedback loops address none of this: nobody shipped a change, nobody doubts the agent's judgement, and the merchants told you immediately.
cases.note: Case 1's failures were invisible and needed observability first; here every failure is already understood and the first move is structural. Ask whether your problem is that you cannot see what happened or that you know exactly what happened and it will happen again.

durable: Read symptoms 1, 2 and 3 together: run state in process memory with 180 runs lost to a deploy, a payment that ran a second time after a crash, and workflow code calling datetime.now() so a replay diverges. What property is missing from this execution model?

A run that spans days with a human approval in the middle cannot live in a process. It needs to be persisted, resumable, safe to replay - and that last one puts constraints on how the workflow code is written.
Durable Execution and Checkpointing. All three pitfalls are in these symptoms: non-deterministic workflow code breaking replay, assuming exactly-once, and checkpointing only at the end.
resilience: Symptom 4: the default ten-minute timeout, hung calls exhausting every worker until the queue stopped, and retries with no budget. What was absent?
Limits on how long you wait, how often you retry, and a way to stop calling a dependency that is already failing - plus a path to fall back to, which must be exercised before the day it matters.
Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Fallbacks. Its three pitfalls are symptom 4 word for word, including untested fallbacks.
incident: Symptom 3's second half and the behaviour around it: traces hold the prompts but not the tool responses, and an engineer edited the prompt in production while refunds were still going out. What goes wrong when you try to investigate?
You cannot reproduce the run, because a re-run fetches today's data rather than that day's. And there is a specific thing you must do before changing anything when money is moving.
Incident Response and Trace Replay. Read all three pitfalls: hot-fixing live while money leaves, traces without tool responses, and a post-mortem that blames a person and adds no test.

drop.canary: A canary limits the damage from a change you ship. Which of these four symptoms was caused by a release?
drop.onlineeval: Online evals catch quality slipping on live traffic. What does the brief say about anyone's opinion of the agent's judgement?
drop.feedback: Feedback loops exist to surface failures users notice but do not report. How did this team find out about the double refunds?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now separate what is finished from what will recur: one of these symptoms was an outage that ended, and two of them will repeat on the next crash and the next deploy.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A ten-minute default timeout let hung calls exhaust every worker and stop the whole queue, which was a total outage.
Runs live in process memory and side effects are not idempotent, so every deploy loses work and every crash can pay a merchant twice.
Traces without tool responses mean no failure here can be reproduced, so nothing can be properly diagnosed.
whyFirst.why: Order by what recurs and what cannot be undone. The queue outage was real and ended; the replay gap makes investigation hard. But money that left twice cannot be recalled by a merchant who has no reason to mention it, and 180 lost runs will become another 180 at the next routine deploy. Both come from the same structural choice, and it is the only one on this list that keeps costing you on a schedule.

cases.title: The copilot that shipped a four-point regression to everyone
cases.brief: A SaaS company's sales copilot drafts outreach emails for 900 reps. Nothing crashes, nothing times out, no provider has changed anything, and each draft is a single short request. The problem is quality, it arrived in a release the team made itself, and it reached every rep at once.
evidence: Prompts are edited in a dashboard by four people, with no review step and no eval gate before they take effect.

A prompt change that passed offline evals went to 100% of traffic in one deploy. Acceptance fell four points, and the dashboard that would have shown it is averaged across all segments, so it stayed invisible until a regional manager complained.

An earlier canary was 0.5% of traffic for one hour - too small to detect a four-point drop - and it ran at 09:00 against a control measured at 22:00. Per-request randomisation also flipped individual reps between variants mid-conversation.

Reps edit about 60% of drafts before sending, and nobody looks at the edits. The only signal collected is thumbs-down, which 0.3% of users ever click. The offline eval set was written eleven months ago.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.versioning: Start here, because everything else on this list assumes the change is a thing you can identify, roll out and roll back - and today it is four people typing into a dashboard with no review and no eval gate. Make the prompt a versioned artefact under review with an eval gate before it takes effect, so a release is an object with an identity rather than an edit that happened. You cannot canary, compare or revert an edit that was never a version.
why.canary: The four-point drop reached every rep because a change that passed offline evals went straight to 100%. Fix all three mistakes the earlier attempt made: size the canary to detect the effect you care about - 0.5% for one hour cannot see four points - compare like with like rather than 09:00 against 22:00, and randomise by user rather than per request so nobody flips variants mid-conversation.
why.feedback: Reps edit 60% of drafts and nobody reads the edits, while the only signal collected is a thumbs-down that 0.3% of people use - so the richest quality signal in the product is being thrown away. Mine the edits, give the loop an owner and a weekly review, and feed real examples into an eval set that is eleven months stale. Handle consent and redaction properly if those conversations become training data.
why.onlineeval: Useful and closely tied to the canary: a dashboard averaged across all segments is how a four-point drop hid until a regional manager called, which is the named pitfall. Alert per segment, over a stable window, with a judge calibrated against human labels.
why.tracing: Useful: per-step traces tagged with the prompt version are what let you attribute a quality change to a release. Mostly in service of the three above.
why.durable: Not needed: a draft is a single short request with no approval wait and no side effect. There is nothing to checkpoint.
why.resilience: Not needed on this evidence: nothing times out, nothing crashes, no provider has slowed down. Timeouts and circuit breakers would protect against a failure mode this product is not having.
why.incident: Not needed as a build: nothing moves money or changes records, and the lesson this module draws for post-mortems - add a test, not a name - is delivered here by the eval gate and the canary you are putting in. Revisit if the copilot ever starts sending by itself.

firstWhy.canary: The right diagnosis of how the damage spread, and your second step - and the earlier attempt is a catalogue of how to do it wrong. But a canary needs two identified variants to compare, and right now a prompt is a dashboard edit with no version and no review, so there is nothing to hold constant as the control.
firstWhy.feedback: The most valuable untapped asset here: 60% of drafts are edited and nobody reads a single one, against a thumbs-down that 0.3% of users click. Build it. But it improves the eval set over weeks, while the next dashboard edit can reach 900 reps this afternoon.
firstWhy.onlineeval: Correct that an average across segments is why this hid until someone phoned - and per-segment alerting is a real gap. It detects the next regression sooner, though, rather than stopping it reaching everybody, and it cannot attribute a drop to a release whose prompt has no version.

cases.model: Start with versioning, because every other control here presumes a change is an identifiable object: take prompts out of a dashboard that four people edit freely, make them reviewed, versioned artefacts with an eval gate before they take effect, and pin the model snapshot. You cannot canary, compare, attribute or revert an edit that was never a version. Then fix the canary, correcting all three errors of the previous attempt: size it to detect a four-point drop rather than 0.5% for an hour, compare the same hours and user groups rather than 09:00 against 22:00, and randomise by user so no rep flips variant mid-conversation. Next build the feedback loop around what reps already do - 60% of drafts are edited and nobody reads the edits, while the only collected signal is a thumbs-down that 0.3% of users click - give it an owner and a weekly review, refresh an eleven-month-old eval set from real examples, and handle consent and redaction before any of it becomes training data. Add online evals alerting per segment rather than on an average, over a stable window, with a calibrated judge, and tag traces with the prompt version so a drop can be attributed to a release. Durable execution, resilience and incident replay address failures this product is not having.
cases.note: Across the three cases the first move went to whatever the other fixes depended on: the record of what ran, the execution model, and here the identity of the change itself. A canary with nothing versioned to compare is as useless as an alert with nothing to attribute it to.

versioning: Symptom 1 looks like process rather than engineering: four people editing prompts in a dashboard, no review, no eval gate. Now look at symptoms 2 and 3 and ask what a canary or a rollback would need that this does not provide.
A change has to be a thing with an identity before it can be gated, compared, attributed or reverted. Two artefacts need that treatment - and one of them is not even under review.
Prompt and Model Versioning. Read the pitfall about prompts edited in a dashboard with no review or eval gate.
canary: Symptom 2: a change that passed offline evals went to 100% of traffic at once. Symptom 3 describes the previous attempt - 0.5% of traffic for an hour, 09:00 canary against a 22:00 control, randomised per request. One technique, four mistakes.
Ship to a slice first. The subtleties are how big the slice must be to see the effect you care about, what you compare it against, and what unit you randomise by.

Canary Releases and Prompt Flags. All three pitfalls are in symptom 3: a canary too small to detect the drop, mismatched hours or groups, and per-request randomisation flipping users mid-conversation.
feedback: Symptom 4: reps edit 60% of drafts and nobody looks at the edits, the only signal is a thumbs-down that 0.3% of users click, and the eval set is eleven months old. What is being wasted?
The users are already telling you what is wrong, in the most detailed form possible, by fixing it themselves. The question is who owns looking at that and what it feeds.
User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel. Read the pitfalls about counting thumbs-down alone, about feedback with no owner or review, and about consent and redaction.

drop.durable: Durable execution protects long tasks with side effects from crashes. How long does drafting one email take, and what does it change?
drop.resilience: Timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks handle a dependency that slows down or fails. Which symptom here describes a failure or a slowdown?
drop.incident: Incident response and trace replay are for an agent misbehaving in production, especially one that moves money or messages customers. What does this copilot do with a draft once it is written?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now ask what two of them need in order to work at all: a canary needs something identifiable to compare against a control, and an alert needs something to attribute a drop to.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A change went to 100% of traffic in one deploy, which is how a four-point drop reached all 900 reps.
A prompt is a dashboard edit with no version, review or gate, so there is nothing to compare, attribute or revert.
60% of drafts are edited and nobody reads the edits, which is the richest quality signal in the product going unused.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the other controls require. Staging the rollout is how you stop the next regression reaching everyone, and the unread edits are the best eval data you will ever get - but a canary needs two identified variants and a stable control, and an alert needs a release to attribute a drop to. While a prompt is an untracked dashboard edit, none of that machinery has anything to grip.

tracing.t: A root span lasts 4.2 s. Its child spans run one after another: a chat span of 1.6 s, a tool span of 0.5 s and a second chat span of 1.7 s. How many seconds of the root span are not covered by any child span?
tracing.a: The children cover 1.6 + 0.5 + 1.7 = 3.8 s, so 4.2 − 3.8 = 0.4 s is spent in your own code between calls: parsing, validation or queueing. That gap is worth a span of its own if it grows.
iv: Why record gen_ai.response.model as well as gen_ai.request.model?

The request says what you asked for; the response says which snapshot actually served it. When you call an alias, the provider can change the snapshot behind it, and only the response attribute reveals that. Grouping failures by it is often the fastest route to the cause of an overnight drop.
Should you capture full prompts and completions in traces?

Not by default. They can contain customer personal data, and the GenAI conventions leave content capture off unless you opt in. Capture content only where you need it, redact personal data first, restrict access, and keep metadata such as tokens, models and errors on every span.
mis: Logging one line per request with no step structure
Emit a span per model call and tool call under one root span
Sampling traces uniformly, so rare errors disappear
Keep every error trace and sample the successful ones

versioning.t: A config uses a model alias. Overnight the provider starts serving a new snapshot to 80% of your traffic. The old snapshot succeeds on 94% of tasks and the new one on 84%. What is your overall success rate now, in percent?
versioning.a: 0.8 × 84 + 0.2 × 94 = 67.2 + 18.8 = 86.0%. An 8-point drop with no deploy on your side; pinning the old snapshot restores 94%.
iv: What belongs in a versioned agent release?

Everything that changes behaviour: the prompt text and version, the model snapshot, the tool definitions and their versions, and generation parameters such as temperature and max tokens. Hash them into one release id and stamp it on every trace, so any answer can be traced to exactly what produced it.
Why not always use the model alias to get improvements automatically?

Because the change arrives untested, on the provider’s schedule, and can shift behaviour your prompts depend on. Pin a dated snapshot, and move to a new one deliberately: run offline evals, then a canary, then promote. Also track the snapshot’s retirement date so the migration is planned.
mis: Editing the live prompt in a dashboard without review
Promote a new version by moving a label only after evals pass
Calling a moving alias in production
Pin a dated snapshot and upgrade through a canary

canary.t: Your service handles 2,000 requests an hour. The canary gets 5% of traffic for 6 hours. If the new prompt is truly 4 points worse, how many extra failed requests will the canary have caused by the end?
canary.a: Canary requests: 2,000 × 0.05 × 6 = 600. Extra failures: 600 × 0.04 = 24. The same change at 100% for 6 hours would have caused 2,000 × 6 × 0.04 = 480.
iv: How do you decide how long a canary must run?

From the smallest drop you care about and your traffic. For a drop from 94% to 90%, a one-sided test with 80% power needs roughly 450 canary requests; at 5% of 2,000 requests an hour that is about 4.5 hours. Also bake long enough to cover the daily traffic mix.
Why bucket by user rather than by request?

So each user sees one variant consistently. Flipping variants mid-conversation confuses users and contaminates metrics, because a failure could come from either version. A hash of a stable id gives sticky, random assignment.
mis: Declaring the canary safe after 50 requests
Size each stage so the drop you care about is detectable
Comparing the canary with last week’s numbers
Compare with a concurrent control group on the same metrics

onlineeval.t: Your agent answers 50,000 questions a day, evenly over 24 hours. A judge scores a random 2% sample. How many judged answers fall in one 6-hour alert window?
onlineeval.a: 50,000 ÷ 24 × 6 = 12,500 answers per window; 2% of that is 250 judged answers. With a 92% pass rate the standard error is about √(0.92 × 0.08 ÷ 250) ≈ 1.7 points, so a 4-point threshold is about 2.3 standard errors.
iv: How is an online eval different from the offline suite?

The offline suite runs fixed test cases before a release; online evals score real traffic after it, continuously. Online evals catch new user behaviour, provider changes and drift the test set never covered, and their failures should be added back to the offline suite.
How do you stop drift alerts from becoming noise?

Use windows large enough for stable estimates, a minimum sample size, thresholds set from the metric’s normal variation, and alerts per important segment rather than only a global average. Review every alert and retune rules that fire without a real problem.
mis: Alerting on every dip in a 15-minute window
Use a window and minimum sample large enough to be stable
Running the judge on 100% of traffic
Check everything cheaply and judge a random sample

durable.t: A ten-step job crashes during step 7. A plain script restarts from step 1, re-running steps 1 to 7. Steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 are model calls of 6,000 tokens each; the rest use no model. How many model tokens does the restart waste?
durable.a: The completed model steps 3 to 6 run again: 4 × 6,000 = 24,000 tokens. A durable workflow replays their recorded results from history instead, and only step 7 runs again.
iv: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?

After a crash the worker replays the workflow code against the event history to rebuild its state. If the code makes different decisions on replay, for example because it reads the clock or a random number, it no longer matches the history. Put all I/O and non-determinism in activities, whose results are recorded.
Does durable execution give exactly-once side effects?

No. An activity can run again if a worker crashes after the side effect but before the result is recorded. Activities are at least once, so payments, emails and tickets need idempotency keys that the receiving system honours.
mis: Sleeping inside a process while waiting days for approval
Wait on a durable signal or timer
Calling APIs directly from workflow code
Do all I/O in activities with timeouts and retry policies

resilience.t: An assistant receives 20 requests a second. During a provider slowdown the average request takes 12 seconds. By Little’s law, how many requests are in flight at once, and does that fit a pool of 200 workers?
resilience.a: In flight = 20 × 12 = 240, which is more than the pool of 200, so requests queue and time out and the whole service degrades. An 8-second timeout with a fast fallback keeps the average near 3 s: 20 × 3 = 60 in flight.
iv: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?

Closed: calls pass through and failures are counted. Open: after a failure threshold, calls fail immediately or go to a fallback, without touching the dependency. Half-open: after a cooldown, a trial call is let through; success closes the breaker, failure opens it again.
Why can retries make an outage worse?

Each retry adds load to a dependency that is already struggling, and with several layers of retries the load multiplies. Use a small retry count with backoff and jitter, a retry budget as a share of traffic, and a circuit breaker so calls stop when failure is persistent.
mis: Keeping the SDK’s 10-minute default timeout
Set a timeout per call below your end-to-end target
Adding a fallback that has never been exercised
Run failure drills that force traffic onto the fallback

incident.t: A refund agent pays duplicate refunds worth ₹60,000 an hour. Merchant complaints surface the problem after 240 minutes; a refund-rate alert would fire after 12. Either way, the kill switch stops the leak 5 minutes after detection. How many rupees does the alert save?
iv: An agent starts doing harm in production. What are your first three moves?

Declare the incident with a severity and one owner. Contain before diagnosing: turn off the harmful tool with a kill switch, or roll the release (prompt, model snapshot, tools and parameters) back to the last good version. Only then investigate, starting from the traces of failing runs. A live prompt hotfix under pressure, without evals, is a guess that can make things worse.
Why can’t you just re-run the failing request to debug it?

A live re-run sees today’s data: the tool that returned PENDING at 10:06 now returns SUCCESS, the model may sample differently, and a refund tool would pay again. A deterministic replay loads the exact release from the trace, uses the same input and parameters, and serves the recorded tool responses instead of calling live APIs, so it reproduces the failure safely. Then the trace becomes an eval case.
mis: Hot-fixing the prompt in production while the incident is live
Flip the kill switch or roll back first; ship the fix later through the normal eval gate
Tracing only inputs and outputs, not tool responses
Record every tool call with its response so the run can be replayed exactly

feedback.t: 2 lakh chats a week; 1.5% leave a rating and 20% of ratings are thumbs-down. How many thumbs-down a week?
iv: How would you use user feedback to improve an assistant?

Capture explicit and implicit signals on traces, triage a sample of negative traces weekly into named failure patterns, turn each into eval cases and a fix with an owner, and add consented, redacted examples to training data; measure each release on the eval set.
Why are implicit signals important?
Few users rate, and those who do are skewed to extremes. Retries, rephrasing, handoffs and edits are far more common and reveal failures users never report.
mis: Relying on thumbs-down alone
Add implicit signals linked to traces
Collecting feedback with no owner
Run a weekly triage with named patterns and owners

gloss: span
One timed operation inside a trace, such as a model call or a tool call, with attributes and a status.
trace
The tree of spans for one request, from the agent invocation down to each model and tool call.
GenAI semantic conventions
OpenTelemetry’s standard names for generative-AI spans, attributes and metrics, such as gen_ai.request.model; still in Development status.
model snapshot
A dated, fixed version of a hosted model. An alias points to a snapshot and can be moved by the provider.
prompt registry
A store of numbered prompt versions with labels such as production, loaded by label from code.
canary release
Sending a change to a small share of live traffic and comparing it with a control group before widening.
feature flag
A runtime switch that decides per user or request which variant of code, prompt or model runs.
online eval
Scoring live production traffic continuously, with cheap checks and a sampled judge.
drift
A change over time in inputs, outputs or quality compared with a reference period.
PSI
Population stability index: a measure of how far a distribution has shifted from a reference.
durable execution
Running a workflow so that each step’s result is recorded and the workflow resumes after crashes without redoing completed steps.
activity
In Temporal, a unit of work with I/O, such as a model or API call, run with timeouts and retries and recorded in history.
circuit breaker
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then probes it before resuming.
MTTR
Mean time to recovery: how long it takes from the start of an incident until service is restored.
deterministic replay
Re-running a recorded agent trace offline with the same input, release and parameters, serving the recorded tool responses instead of calling live systems, to reproduce a failure safely.
blameless post-mortem
A written review after an incident that records the timeline, impact, causes and owned actions, and looks for system fixes rather than people to blame.
incident severity
An agreed scale, such as SEV1 to SEV3, that sets how fast people are paged and who is involved, based on the harm happening now.
implicit feedback
Signals from user behaviour, such as retries, rephrasing, copying, abandoning or asking for a human.
data flywheel
A loop where product use produces data that improves the product, which brings more use.
failure pattern
A named, counted cluster of similar failures found during triage.

onlineeval.name: System-Level Eval
onlineeval.note: System-level evals run offline before release; online evals keep scoring the same qualities on live traffic after it.

onlineeval.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
onlineeval.note: The sampled judge in online evals must be calibrated against human labels, exactly as in LLM-as-a-judge.

onlineeval.name: Eval Datasets
onlineeval.note: Online evaluation of live traffic finds new failures; each one, redacted and labelled, becomes a case in the next version of the offline set.

onlineeval.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
onlineeval.note: Online eval scores and drift alerts are detection signals that open an incident, and each confirmed failure flows back as a new test case.

onlineeval.name: User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel
onlineeval.note: Online evals score sampled traffic automatically; user feedback shows which failures people actually notice.

tracing.name: Process-Level Eval
tracing.note: Process-level evaluation grades the steps of a run, and traces are where those steps are recorded.

tracing.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
tracing.note: Token counts on every span show which steps and tools drive cost, the input for step caps and tool pruning.

tracing.name: Audit Trails and Explainability
tracing.note: Traces show how an agent behaved for engineers; an audit trail turns the same data into a tamper-evident decision record for auditors and regulators.

tracing.name: PII Detection and Redaction
tracing.note: Traces copy every prompt and tool result; redact before spans are exported, not only before the model call.

tracing.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
tracing.note: Per-stage p50 and p95 come from traces: a span for each LLM call, tool and retrieval shows where the seconds go.

tracing.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
tracing.note: Replay needs traces that record every tool call with its response; tracing supplies the evidence, incident response uses it under pressure.

resilience.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
resilience.note: Safe retries make one call repeatable; timeouts, breakers and fallbacks protect the whole system when a dependency keeps failing.

resilience.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
resilience.note: The timeout-and-fallback lever is a resilience pattern; the budget adds how tight the timeout may be and how many degraded answers are acceptable.

resilience.name: Third-Party and Vendor Model Risk
resilience.note: A tested second provider behind one gateway is the fallback pattern from resilience, used here to manage concentration risk on a single vendor.

durable.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
durable.note: Durable workflows run activities at least once, so side-effecting activities still need idempotency keys.

durable.name: LangGraph
durable.note: LangGraph’s checkpointer is one way to get the durable execution that long agent runs need.

durable.name: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
durable.note: A paused run is only as safe as its saved state: durable checkpointing lets it wait hours and survive deploys.

canary.name: System-Level Eval
canary.note: Offline system-level evals are the gate before a canary; the canary is the last check on live traffic.

canary.name: Automated Red Teaming
canary.note: Run the red-team regression suite as a release gate before a canary starts.

canary.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
canary.note: Offline evals decide whether a tuned model may ship; a canary on a slice of live traffic confirms it before full rollout.

versioning.name: Model Routing and Tiering
versioning.note: A routed system has one release per route: pin the snapshot for each model tier and version them together.

versioning.name: Prompt Templates and Regression Tests
versioning.note: Templates and regression tests make a prompt change safe to write; a registry and trace stamps make it safe to ship and roll back.

versioning.name: Audit Trails and Explainability
versioning.note: Each decision record should carry the model and prompt versions that the registry assigns.

versioning.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
versioning.note: Rolling back to the last good release is only a label move when prompt, snapshot, tools and parameters are versioned together.

versioning.name: Third-Party and Vendor Model Risk
versioning.note: Pinning a dated model snapshot and re-running evals before any change is prompt and model versioning applied to a provider you do not control.

incident.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
incident.note: Replay needs traces that record every tool call with its response; tracing supplies the evidence, incident response uses it under pressure.

incident.name: Prompt and Model Versioning
incident.note: Rolling back to the last good release is only a label move when prompt, snapshot, tools and parameters are versioned together.

incident.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
incident.note: The duplicate-refund incident had a contributing cause: no idempotency key per order, so a repeated refund call was paid twice.

incident.name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
incident.note: Online eval scores and drift alerts are detection signals that open an incident, and each confirmed failure flows back as a new test case.

incident.name: Cost Attribution and Budget Guards
incident.note: Spend spikes by tag are an incident signal like error rates.

incident.name: AI Incident Management and Reporting
incident.note: Incident Response restores service and replays traces; AI incident management decides severity, notifications and closure.

feedback.name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
feedback.note: Online evals score sampled traffic automatically; user feedback shows which failures people actually notice.

feedback.name: Eval Datasets
feedback.note: Triage patterns become new eval cases, keeping the eval set close to real use.

feedback.name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
feedback.note: Consented, redacted feedback examples become curated fine-tuning or preference data.

gifs.canary: Prompt v13 goes to 5% of traffic behind a flag; after 600 conversations it resolves 90% against 94% for control, so the guardrail rolls it back after 24 extra failures instead of 480.
gifs.durable: A ten-step claim crashes at step 7; a plain script restarts from step 1 and redoes 24,000 tokens, while a durable workflow replays steps 1 to 6 from history and continues.
gifs.feedback: Four signals appear: thumbs on 1.5 percent of chats, retries, rephrasing and requests for a human. A weekly triage turns 300 traces into named failure patterns: COD refund status in Hinglish with 64 traces, pincode not serviceable with 41, and wrong courier partner with 28. Each pattern becomes 20 eval cases, an owner, a fix and consented training data. Resolution rises from 72 to 79 percent, and a pattern goes from first sighting to fix in 10 days instead of 45.
gifs.incident: An animated scene titled Incident Response. On the left, a chart of refunds per order in 10-minute windows sits at a 2.1% baseline until prompt v8 goes live at 10:00; the line then climbs to 4.4%, crossing a dashed alert line at 3.15%, and a red label reads "4.4% · SEV1". Next, a Contain panel appears on the right: a switch for the issue_refund tool flips from ON to OFF, a note says refunds queue for people from 10:17, and a chip shows the release moving from rel-v8 back to rel-v7, while the chart line falls back to the baseline. Finally, a replay band along the bottom shows trace tr-4f91 replayed offline with the same input, prompt v8 at temperature 0 and recorded tool responses; the result, "issue_refund ×2", is marked as a failure, a note says 10 of 10 replays pay twice on v8 while v7 pays once, and a green chip adds the case to the eval set.
gifs.onlineeval: Cheap checks run on every answer and a judge scores 2%; the daily pass rate holds near 92% for a week, then falls to 86% below the 88% alert line and pages on-call.
gifs.resilience: With SDK defaults a failing provider ties up 7,525 workers and takes the service down; 8-second timeouts free the workers, and a circuit breaker with a secondary provider answers 97% with a p95 of 3 seconds.
gifs.tracing: A claim's trace appears as a tree of spans; grouping failures by region shows every group near 86%, while grouping by the served model shows 94% on the old snapshot and 84% on the new one.
gifs.versioning: A release bundles prompt v12, a pinned snapshot, tools and parameters; when the provider moves the alias, the aliased config drops to 86% while the pinned one stays at 94%, and a bad prompt is rolled back in 2 minutes by a label move instead of 45 by redeploy.

header.lede: Evaluation tells you something broke. AgentOps tells you what broke, who shipped it, and how to recover: trace every run, version every release, ship changes to a slice of traffic first, score live traffic, survive crashes, and fail gracefully when a provider does.
